item.title: Vitamin K Refusal Rates Have Doubled, and Infant Brain Hemorrhage Is Preventable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-tpwky-维生素-k-注射被拒率翻倍-婴儿脑出血本可避免/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-tpwky-维生素-k-注射被拒率翻倍-婴儿脑出血本可避免/
item.description: Every newborn is physiologically deficient in vitamin K at birth, and a single intramuscular injection drops the risk of late bleeding to near zero; but US refusal rates have risen from 3% to 5.8%, and babies whose parents refuse have 81 times the risk of late bleeding.
item.content:encoded:
Every newborn is physiologically deficient in vitamin K at birth, and a single intramuscular injection drops the risk of late bleeding to near zero; but US refusal rates have risen from 3% to 5.8%, and babies whose parents refuse have 81 times the risk of late bleeding.

High information density: it covers both the clinical mechanics of newborn hemorrhage and the history of vitamin K's discovery and how a 1950s overdose scandal destroyed trust. The second half, on who refuses and why communication fails, is the most valuable part.

20:34 Every newborn is born deficient in vitamin K
Vitamin K does not cross the placenta effectively, so even if the mother supplements during pregnancy, the newborn's vitamin K-dependent clotting factors do not rise appreciably. Add an immature gut microbiome and very little endogenous K2 synthesis, and breast milk averaging only about 2.5 micrograms per liter, and an exclusively breastfed infant takes in less than 1 microgram a day for the first six months. The result is that every newborn is at high risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding. This is not an outlier phenomenon; it is the physiological norm.

22:35 Late bleeding often comes with no warning, straight to brain hemorrhage
Vitamin K deficiency bleeding in newborns comes in three types: early, within 24 hours of birth; classic, within the first week; and late, from one week to six months. Late is the most dangerous: about 60% of cases are intracranial hemorrhage, and there is often no warning bleed beforehand, just sudden brain hemorrhage, seizures or unresponsiveness. Mortality ranges from 50% to 60% depending on era and country, with modern figures around 20%. That is why the value of a single preventive shot cannot be measured by "the bleeding probability is low."

25:46 One intramuscular shot pushes the risk to near zero
Since 2003 in the US, and in the vast majority of medical societies and public health agencies worldwide, a single intramuscular vitamin K injection at birth has been recommended. It provides a stable supply for the first few months and cuts the risk of late bleeding from 4 to 7 cases per 100,000 live births (some countries report as high as 80) to about 0.4. Infants who receive no prophylaxis have 81 times the risk of late bleeding compared with those who do. Oral regimens also significantly reduce risk, but they require multiple doses, are affected by absorption and vomiting, and are less effective than injection; the US has no regulator-approved oral formulation.

44:27 How a 1950s overdose scandal destroyed trust
In the postwar research climate, informed consent and patient protections had not yet entered the picture, and the logic was "vitamin is harmless and possibly beneficial, so give it to all premature infants." In the mid-1950s Britain gave some premature infants up to 60 milligrams of synthetic vitamin K, after which jaundice, hemolysis and kernicterus rose, and several infants died. The formulation was withdrawn and the dose dropped back to 1 milligram, but confidence had been shaken: of more than 16,000 infants born in Britain in a single week in 1970, only 20% received vitamin K. This history shows that the aftershocks of a single overdose incident can last for decades.

46:31 The 1990s leukemia scare has never fully cleared
In the early 1990s two British studies linked intramuscular vitamin K to later leukemia risk, and the reaction was swift and strong: some countries switched to recommending oral regimens and reserved injections for the highest-risk infants, and British injection rates fell from 58% in 1988 to 38% in 1993. But the two studies had small samples and insufficient controls, and a large body of subsequent research and a WHO working group found no association; IARC also concluded there was no evidence of carcinogenicity. The problem is that bad news travels fast and good news does not, just like MMR and autism: once doubt is planted, the world never fully recovers.

49:35 Refusal rates have doubled, and the 81-fold risk is badly underestimated
US refusal rates nearly doubled from 2017 to 2024, rising from 3% to 5.8%, with some hospitals reporting higher. Infants whose parents refuse have 81 times the risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding, and that figure is badly underestimated because the bleeding itself remains rare and communication is inadequate. Research shows most parents, whether they accept or refuse, know vitamin K is related to bleeding, but do not know that this bleeding can cause severe brain injury and a mortality risk above 20%. The information is present, but it is not being effectively conveyed.

50:36 Refusal reasons fall into three categories, and birth attendants matter enormously
Refusal reasons fall roughly into three categories: distrust of medicine, pursuit of "natural birth," and preference for alternative medical lifestyles. Some argue that if infants needed more vitamin K, evolution or God would have provided it; others read a recommendation to supplement vitamin K as "you are not fit to be a mother." Research also finds refusers are more likely to be white, college-educated, over 30, and planning a home or birth-center delivery. The birth attendant's stance is critical: in a New Zealand survey, 100% of doctors thought all infants should receive vitamin K, while only 55% of midwives did, and 26% of those would not give it to their own children; in Canada, infants delivered by midwives were 8 times more likely to have vitamin K refused than those delivered by doctors.

55:46 Doctors are seeing newborns bleed to death for the first time
Some parents who lost a child or whose child suffered brain injury because vitamin K was not given are doing something very brave: saying publicly, "I made this decision, this is the consequence, don't do what I did." At the same time, doctors are seeing newborns bleed to death for the first time in their careers, and they are raising the alarm in their communities. Some researchers and doctors are pushing to establish a national US registry of vitamin K refusal and administration, because vitamin K deficiency bleeding is not a notifiable disease and cases are likely undercounted. In a post-pandemic era when expertise is treated as a dirty word, these preventable injuries and deaths will keep increasing.

item.title: Procrastination Is Not a Willpower Problem: You'll Fail With the Same Plan Next Time
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-clearerthink-拖延不是意志力问题-下次你还会用同一个计划失败/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-clearerthink-拖延不是意志力问题-下次你还会用同一个计划失败/
item.description: Procrastination is delaying despite knowing it's harmful, and about 20% of adults do it chronically. Anxiety, distraction, burnout and perfectionism each need different fixes, but they share one premise: without changing the plan, the result won't change.
item.content:encoded:
Procrastination is delaying despite knowing it's harmful, and about 20% of adults do it chronically. Anxiety, distraction, burnout and perfectionism each need different fixes, but they share one premise: without changing the plan, the result won't change.

It breaks procrastination into types you can treat, and gives a concrete, actionable toolbox rather than another 'self-discipline' pep talk. Medium-to-high information density.

1:16 The definition of procrastination hides reluctance
Itamar's definition is: we delay something even though we don't intend to delay it, and we know it's bad for us. So 'actively deciding to do it later and feeling fine about it' is not procrastination. The gray area is: does it count when you think delaying is good for you but it's actually harmful? His test is 'could you have expected this to be better for you.' About 20% of adults procrastinate chronically, and among students it's 50%. He stresses that procrastination doesn't only happen to people who don't care; people high in conscientiousness, genuinely productive, who really want to make an impact, procrastinate too.

3:27 Procrastination is many types, not one thing
Treating procrastination as a single phenomenon makes two mistakes at once: you fail to see that it happens to people other than students, and you can't deal with it in practice. Because a student who procrastinates from distraction, an executive who procrastinates from burnout, and an artist who procrastinates from perfectionism have different drivers and need different solutions. In his book Itamar distinguishes anxiety-driven, pulled-away-by-external-temptation, and burnout-driven types, plus a category he calls zigzaggers—closer to ADHD and impulsivity, switching back and forth between internal rather than external distractions.

5:00 Anxiety has two faces: fear of the task or fear of the consequences
The mechanism by which anxiety causes procrastination is: doing this hurts, the brain says I don't want to hurt, so you push it away. But anxiety also has an adaptive side—if what you're anxious about isn't the task itself but the consequences of not finishing it, a little anxiety actually pushes you to act. The key variables are intensity and self-efficacy: a little anxiety may motivate you, a lot of anxiety paralyzes you no matter what it's aimed at; and if you also feel you're incapable of finishing, anxiety more easily turns into paralysis. Itamar adds: even when anxiety drives you, it's a dangerous source of motivation, because it also brings stress and a worse experience.

9:25 The biggest mistake is believing you'll try harder next time
Itamar says the biggest mistake people make when tackling procrastination is falling into the self-control fallacy: believing that next time, if you just try harder and use more willpower, you'll get it done. The absurdity is that we see it fail again and again, yet believe it again and again. The reasons include the bias blind spot (failing to recognize your own biases) and the empathy gap (predicting, in a calm state, what you'll do when you're in a hot emotional state). The real harm of this belief is that it offers a superficially minimal silver bullet, which stops you from looking for what actually works. Spencer's addition: if nothing changes, the result won't change.

12:45 Design for your future self as if they were someone else
Spencer's approach is: don't assume that the you of two weeks from now will get it done on willpower, but ask 'for someone a lot like me, what would help them get this done in two weeks'—set reminders, make social commitments, add rewards. Itamar says this is exactly an illustration of his core claim: procrastination is not a time management problem, and even excellent time management can fail; what you should do is distance management. Calling yourself in the second or third person, or using your name instead of 'I', or asking 'what advice would I give a friend', all create psychological distance and help you enter wise reasoning, see through the situation and bypass biases.

16:13 Anxiety type: decatastrophize, or do it anxious
For anxiety-driven procrastinators, Itamar's first choice is to decatastrophize: catastrophizing is overestimating the probability that something bad will happen and also overestimating how much it will hurt you. For example, 'there's a typo in the proposal, so the agent will blacklist me, and will tell everyone to blacklist me too.' The method is to ask: how likely is this to happen? If it did happen, how big would the impact be? If it happened, how could I carry on? Spencer offers an almost opposite strategy: notice that this task makes me anxious, sit in that feeling, feel it, and then do it anyway, which he calls metacognitive awareness. Itamar files it under the umbrella of mindfulness and self-compassion.

21:39 Procrastination is short-term emotional repair, and it self-reinforces
Spencer points out that anxiety creates anxiety: once you say 'I won't do it now', the anxiety usually drops immediately, and you're learning that 'procrastinating makes me feel better', forming a reinforcement loop. Doing the opposite can undo it—doing it while anxious is effectively an exposure. Itamar says procrastination here is a defense mechanism: because you feel pressure or anxiety about what you should do, you push it away to avoid the painful emotion. It makes you feel good in the short term and worse in the long term, because you haven't solved the problem, you've only made yourself face it repeatedly later, or face worse consequences.

26:39 The burnout fix is to do less
Itamar admits this is the last thing burned-out people want to hear: if you're burned out because you're doing too much, doing things that drain you, you probably need to do less and take more deliberate care of yourself—specifically, more deliberately deciding what to do and, more importantly, what not to do. He describes a loop: you're used to performing well, burnout makes your performance worse, so you work even harder, then burn out more, and it gets worse and worse. He calls this 'borrowing health and productivity from your future self.' He also notes that burnout doesn't only come from hours: reasonable hours but high-pressure, meaningless, or otherwise draining tasks can also burn you out.

item.title: Optimism Is Not a Personality Trait, It's an Explanatory Style You Can Train
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-hiddenbrain-乐观不是性格-是一套可以练的解释风格/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-hiddenbrain-乐观不是性格-是一套可以练的解释风格/
item.description: Helplessness is learned, and so is optimism. What decides whether a person gives up is not the blow itself but whether he explains it as permanent, pervasive, or his own fault.
item.content:encoded:
Helplessness is learned, and so is optimism. What decides whether a person gives up is not the blow itself but whether he explains it as permanent, pervasive, or his own fault.

Seligman himself walks through the full chain from learned helplessness to learned optimism, and in the back half treats agency as a civilizational variable and tries to quantify it — a rare angle.

9:36 The dog doesn't run, and it's not because it never learned to run
In Solomon's lab, on day one the dog was strapped into a hammock and given Pavlovian shocks it could not escape no matter what it did; on day two it was put in a shuttle box where running to the other side would turn off the shock, and the dog just lay there. Seligman's judgment was that what the animal actually learned was not "the tone predicts the shock" but "nothing I do matters." That reading was in direct conflict with behaviorism at the time, because it required the animal to be a cognitive subject capable of thinking and integrating experience across time.

13:50 People can be taught to give up by noise, too
Hiroto moved the same design onto humans: on day one, headphones playing a harsh noise, with one group unable to turn it off no matter what they pressed and another group able to stop it with a button. On day two came a four-foot "human shuttle box" — hand on one side and the noise sounds, move it to the other side and it stops. People who had been through uncontrollable noise the day before kept their hand in the box and did nothing. Seligman stresses that the variable doing the work is not the trauma itself but whether there was control over the trauma — and they ran control experiments on exactly this point.

19:00 Helplessness became the model for depression
In 1970 depression was not yet a diagnostic category; there was only "manic-depressive illness." By 1975 the American Psychiatric Association's DSM had for the first time split out "unipolar depression," listing nine symptoms: passivity, cognitive difficulty, sadness, anxiety, sleep problems, food losing its taste, numbness, loss of pleasure, thoughts of death. Seligman compared the nine symptoms against the learned-helplessness literature that had accumulated by then and found that eight of the nine could be reproduced in the lab; the only one missing was thoughts of death — probably because the experiments used noise rather than something more severe. That model went on to become the dominant model of depression, and the drugs that could break helplessness in the lab became the mainstream antidepressants.

22:19 Five out of eight give up; a third never do
Across the whole helplessness literature the effect is statistical: on average five out of eight people or eight rats become helpless, and about a third do not. From the 1970s on, Seligman kept asking what was different about that third, and it became the turning point of his career. The answer landed on explanatory style: people who explain bad events as permanent ("I'm stupid"), pervasive ("I'm unlovable"), and their own fault become helpless; people who explain them as temporary, local, and not their fault recover quickly.

26:50 West Point's first week already predicts who drops out
The first six weeks after arriving at West Point are called Beast Barracks: woken at four in the morning to run ten miles, systematically put through the wringer, with the stated purpose being to "break them," and roughly a third of candidates quit. Seligman's team measured explanatory style on day one, and the ones who dropped out were the pessimists. The same pattern shows up in college grades (optimists outperform their talent, pessimists underperform it) and in insurance sales: MetLife lost 50% of new hires within a year and 90% within four years; they hired 140 "special forces" whose optimism-scale scores were off the charts, and this group outsold the whole company, with 75% still on the job after four years while the ordinary group was down to 10%.

34:17 Agency breaks into three beliefs
Seligman defines agency as the opposite of learned helplessness, made up of three parts: efficacy, the belief that you can accomplish a specific goal right here and now; optimism, the belief that you can accomplish it not only now but in the future and the further future; and imagination, the range of possible goals you can imagine — the wider the range, the stronger the agency. Full agency is: I can do it now, I can do it in the future, and I can innovate across many different situations.

36:22 The axial age's answer may have been "I can do it"
Between 1000 and 500 BC, Greece, the Hebrew world, China, India, and Persia all underwent upheaval: the Buddha, Confucius, and Socrates appeared, and technology, medicine, art, literature, and the first political freedoms all erupted together. Seligman's hypothesis is that over those five centuries humanity discovered the concept of agency. The evidence is vocabulary: in the Iliad, Achilles does not decide to act on his own — Athena tells him to act; a hundred years later, in the Odyssey, Odysseus is already a wily, resourceful man who makes his own decisions, and the gods begin to exit the stage. By 500 BC, every culture had produced a large vocabulary of human agency.

38:30 In the Old Testament, the verbs God commands with are dwindling
Seligman took the entire Old Testament and counted agency verbs: roughly speaking, in the Pentateuch God commands and people obey, with only a few exceptions like "choose life"; the further you go, into the Prophets and the Writings, the more words for human agency appear and the fewer for divine agency. You can now have AI score each book for agency, and plotted by time it comes out linear — from the Pentateuch to the Babylonian exile around 300 BC, agency increases, and it correlates linearly with human innovation, population, living standards, political freedom, and technology.

item.title: He Never Won Elected Office, Yet He Reshaped All of New York
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-stuffmissed-他从未当选任何公职-却重塑了整座纽约/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-stuffmissed-他从未当选任何公职-却重塑了整座纽约/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Robert Moses stacked appointed positions into power, rewrote New York with parks and highways, and wrote racial bias into the city's fabric — his legacy is still being argued over today.
item.content:encoded:
Robert Moses stacked appointed positions into power, rewrote New York with parks and highways, and wrote racial bias into the city's fabric — his legacy is still being argued over today.

This episode is medium-density on information, but how Moses accumulated power through unelected posts, and the exact words from his 1945 Atlantic Monthly article, are valuable for understanding urban governance and how power actually operates.

1:01 Never elected, yet he held enormous power
Robert Moses was never elected to any public office in his life, yet he accumulated enormous power by being appointed to a range of government positions. According to Encyclopaedia Britannica, his work includes 35 highways, 12 bridges, numerous parks, Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts, Shea Stadium, many housing projects, two hydroelectric plants, and the 1964 New York World's Fair. He has been dead 45 years and remains a divisive figure, and his legacy may be argued over for another century or more.

6:10 His mentor taught him not to anger voters
Moses became chief of staff of the New York State Reconstruction Commission in 1919 and learned a great deal from Belle Moskovitz. Moskovitz understood deeply how to maneuver within government to achieve goals without antagonizing those in power. One example: in an early draft of a report, Moses suggested cutting part of the workforce, and Moskovitz reminded him that every one of those people was a voter, that they could not be angered, and that he had to find a way to cut costs without cutting that many jobs. This ‘don't anger the voters’ thinking ran through his later government work.

11:11 Parks were the means, highways were the end
When Moses took over the parks commission, most green-space plans simply preserved natural wilderness, but he envisioned adding more manicured landscaping and dedicated recreation areas. More importantly, every time he built a new park, he made sure the project included roads connecting the park to highways — that is where the parkway came from. From the start he planned a large state park system for Long Island, all linked by new roads. In just four years in the job, he added 13 parks to Long Island, totaling about 9,700 acres, where previously there had been only one park.

13:14 His mother lent him $20,000 to save Jones Beach
Jones Beach was originally just a sandbar on the southern edge of Long Island, almost completely submerged at high tide. Moses wanted to turn it into a great park, and most of the government and the press considered it impractical. He first used large-scale dredging to pull about 40 million cubic yards of sand from the seabed, raising the sandbar from two feet above sea level to twelve feet. But the project nearly died when the money ran out, and Moses did something highly unusual: he borrowed $20,000 from his mother, Bella, to keep the work going. He later confirmed that if his mother had not put up the money, the contractor would not have brought the equipment back to finish. Jones Beach finally opened on August 4, 1925, in a dust storm, and an estimated 1.5 million people visited in its first year.

22:31 His only campaign, and he lost badly
Moses ran for public office only once in his life. In 1934 he ran for governor of New York and was thoroughly defeated by the incumbent Democratic governor, Herbert H. Lehman. Lehman received more than 2.2 million popular votes; Moses got fewer than 1.4 million. Reporting Lehman's victory, The New York Times wrote: ‘Meanwhile, his formidable and combative opponent, Robert Moses, will be free to continue his work as the great parks commissioner.’ After this defeat he never tried campaigning again, and instead kept expanding his power through appointed positions.

23:33 235 new playgrounds, only one in Harlem
Starting in the 1930s, Moses greatly expanded the city's playgrounds, building 235 new ones. But a pattern began to emerge: he ignored the needs of districts with predominantly non-white populations. Of the 235 playgrounds, only one was in Harlem. In the summer of 1936 he opened 11 new swimming pools: 4 in Manhattan (including one in Harlem and one in West Harlem), 4 in Brooklyn, and 1 each in the Bronx, Queens, and Staten Island. These pools had new filtration and chlorination systems, heating, and underwater lighting, and were considered advanced, but they were also designed to be drained in the cooler months and used for other activities, from shuffleboard to roller skating.

24:35 ‘Tear down the slums, just build a road’
In a 1945 article in The Atlantic Monthly, Moses opened by describing how slums form: existing buildings become overcrowded, speculators add tenants, and people are packed into tenements like chickens. But the ‘therapy’ he offered was this: clearing slums in most cities is done indirectly — not for public, semi-public, or private housing, but for parks, playgrounds, parkways, highways, boulevards, and other public improvements. He boasted that his ‘demolition-and-construction demon squad’ had torn down more old slums than all the housing experts combined, and that ‘we built nothing but broad highways, lined with landscaping and recreational facilities.’

33:43 Eminent domain is the only salvation
In the article Moses explicitly endorsed the use of eminent domain to acquire land. He wrote that buying large tracts at reasonable prices had become impossible, and that in such a situation, ‘eminent domain is the only salvation.’ Condemnation had to be exercised by the city, state, or federal government for private limited-dividend or redevelopment companies. He also criticized unions as ‘a serious obstacle to financing slum clearance,’ accusing them of insisting on retaining hourly-wage rights, striking, and ‘resisting invention and improvement in the building field.’ He said this attitude was ‘without justification’ and would not change until a better-educated new generation of union officials appeared.

item.title: Chinese open-weight models lead, and distillation only explains a one-to-two-month gap

item.description: Chinese models lead across the board on downloads and benchmarks, but distillation only explains a one-to-two-month gap — the real reasons are release cadence and task focus; US companies are already building products on Chinese models.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese models lead across the board on downloads and benchmarks, but distillation only explains a one-to-two-month gap — the real reasons are release cadence and task focus; US companies are already building products on Chinese models.

This is a state-of-open-models briefing for Congress: dense with data and clear in its judgments, suited to anyone who wants to grasp the US-China open-model landscape quickly.

0:00 Open weights is not the same as open source
An open-weight model releases only the weights and a license; an open-source model also releases the training code and data. America's genuinely open-source models are led by nonprofits, such as the Allen Institute for AI's Olmo, OpenAthena's Marin, and EleutherAI's Pythia. Nvidia's Nemotron is more open than most open-weight models, having released a large amount of training data, but because it has not released all of it, it still does not count as fully open source. The distinction matters: when people discuss ‘open source’, what they are actually talking about is mostly open weights.

0:00 Chinese models have crossed the agentic-capability threshold
GLM-5.2 and Kimi K3 achieved a step change in commercial viability, crossing an agentic-capability threshold similar to the one Anthropic's Claude Code crossed in December 2025. Chinese open-weight models overtook the US in these two key areas roughly 18 months ago. On Hugging Face downloads, China took the lead in July 2025, mainly on the back of Alibaba's Qwen. Data from the ATOM project, which the author maintains, shows China's download lead has grown to about 1.6 billion out of a total of 3.2 billion, twice that of the US.

0:00 The benchmark gap is stark
On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, as of September 14, 2026, the top three are Chinese models: Z.ai's GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash score 45 and 42, and Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 scores 44. The US leaders are Thinking Machines' Inkling and Inkling Small, both scoring 26, and Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra at 23. The top US models were released in June and July 2026, and refresh less often than their Chinese counterparts. Chinese labs are closest on tasks with well-defined demand, such as agentic coding, and lag further behind on open-ended scientific tasks like physics and biology.

0:00 Distillation only explains a one-to-two-month gap
Distillation is a technique Chinese labs use often, training their own models on the outputs of stronger models, but the author estimates that even if distillation were blocked entirely — say by deploying KYC tools at Anthropic and OpenAI — the gap from the strongest US models to Chinese open-weight models would widen by only 1-2 months. Distillation matters most in new domains, and it cannot easily produce a comprehensively strong final model. Chinese labs ship faster and have a narrower task distribution, which slightly inflates scores on public benchmarks, because every lab keeps improving and later-released models naturally score higher.

0:00 US companies are building products on Chinese models
Harvey, Cursor and DoorDash use Kimi; Airbnb uses Qwen; Perplexity uses DeepSeek. A large number of young Silicon Valley startups use Chinese models to get a low-cost, flexible option. US startups sign enterprise agreements with Chinese model labs to license products for use, a new form of cross-border technology cooperation the author has not seen in his career. On OpenRouter, the Chinese model share has grown from about 70% to more than 80%, and weekly tokens processed have grown from about 1 trillion in September 2025 to about 80 trillion today. On OpenCode, Chinese models account for about 95% or more of inference volume.

0:00 Academia has already been taken over by Qwen
The author scanned papers in the five most popular ML categories on arXiv (cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.CV, cs.LG, stat.ML). In January 2023, 2% of papers mentioned any open model; by September 2026 that reached 50%. In April-May 2023, of about 12,000 new papers, 2,600 mentioned at least one open-model family, 5.5% mentioned Llama and 1% mentioned Chinese models. At Llama's peak in fall 2024, 23% mentioned Llama and 7.5% mentioned Qwen. Today Llama is still mentioned by about 21% of papers, while Qwen has risen to 30%. Any Chinese open-weight model is mentioned by more than 40% of papers, versus 30% for the US.

0:00 US models see higher adoption at equal capability
Research shows that US models are adopted disproportionately more at comparable capability and scale. OpenAI's gpt-oss, its first open-weight models since ChatGPT, became one of the most widely adopted open-weight models ever. Google's Gemma 4 is one of the few models whose adoption approaches Qwen's most popular small models. Nvidia's Nemotron, despite being more capable at the same scale, has seen middling adoption. This shows US models have brand and ecosystem advantages, but not enough to reverse the overall trend.

0:00 Open-model risk requires ecosystem-level preparation
The structural challenge of open-weight models is that there is almost no effective way to stop pieces of open-source software from falling into the wrong hands. If access to China's strongest open-weight models were restricted over risk, it would be US companies that suffer. HuggingFace once used a Chinese open-weight model to understand a cyberattack, because closed models refused the request. Managing open-weight model risk usually comes down to ecosystem preparation. Open models are becoming an essential tool for AI diffusion, and continuing to invest in US open models is the best path to staying ahead of these risks.

item.content:encoded:
Banning books and telling teachers what they can't teach strikes at the root of free expression just like censoring the news; who a collective is and what it values takes shape through language — art is democracy's infrastructure, not its poster.

Not a literature class: a working poet who heads the largest humanities funder in the country explains why close reading, naming and literacy are political capacities; the second half is harder than the opening.

5:32 The poet went to the scene instead of writing reflections
Rukeyser was not a poet who stayed in her study. At 19, while studying at Vassar, she felt she had to go south to sit in on the Scottsboro trial — staying at school was simply not an option; in 1936 she went to Spain to see the anti-Olympics mounted against the Berlin Games, arriving just as the Spanish Civil War broke out; she also went to West Virginia to write about the Hawks Nest mine disaster — Union Carbide dug tunnels without wet drilling and without giving workers protective gear, the workers were mostly African American, and nearly all died of silicosis, which Alexander says may be the largest corporate industrial accident in American history. The conclusion: writing lets more people know what happened, and connects people of different identities on shared human experience.

13:50 Art is a pillar of democracy, not an illustration
She breaks democracy down into a question of language: who a collective is, what it values, which voices it has, all take shape through language, so without language there is no collective. When we talk about free speech we always fixate on journalism, but artists being censored, books being banned, teachers being told what they can teach strike at the same root. Her wording is hard: art is not democracy's explanatory diagram, art is itself part of democracy — one of its pillars. And poetry doesn't just wave a flag for values; it is the thing itself. To judge whether a democracy is healthy, look at whether art can still occupy an unconstrained space.

33:37 Close reading is critical thinking, and it can be taught
She puts close reading very plainly: a method, a practice, anyone can learn it, and its other name is critical thinking. Its use isn't limited to poetry — you can use it reading the newspaper, reading the propaganda around you, whether that propaganda comes from above or from advertising and very, very powerful culture. Figuring out how others are working on you is a good thing. And in America many people are nervous about poetry, feeling they ‘aren't supposed to understand it’; her method is concrete: drop your shoulders, read it again, don't just read it on the page, read it aloud, then you read it to me — the same poem read by a different person, and you hear something different every time.

42:37 Misnaming people is an anti-democratic weapon
She says one of the most powerful weapons against democracy is misnaming people, calling people by the wrong name. In America there's a saying, calling people out of their names, meaning flattening people, using insulting labels, even smearing the behavior of an entire people wholesale — this is abuse of language, its purpose is to wound and divide, and it is coming from the highest levels of government. She stresses one thing in particular: it has real consequences. Conversely, naming things precisely, saying what you mean, saying who you are, and catching what others say, are themselves the capacities democracy needs.

47:58 Writing grief into language is the only way to hold it
Her husband Fikre died 14 years ago. She wrote a memoir shortly after his death, which surprised even her — she never thought she would write it or show it to anyone; it was more a way of landing, of knowing what she was going through: too overwhelming, too unprecedented, and turning some of it into language helped her name the feeling. Writing about him years later was different in kind, became a responsibility: this person was her ‘my person’, who lived a brave, extraordinary, beautiful life and left hundreds of paintings, now shown in museums and galleries. She is wary of herself too: she hopes she isn't wringing this experience dry.

57:30 Writing poetry throws away far more than it keeps
She doesn't start a poem from ‘I'm going to write a poem about X’, but from a word, an image, a phrase that rings there, and she can't say why, so she writes it down again and again. She has a day job — almost all poets do — so the real question is: while you're busy with something else, where do you put the thought down. Fragments accumulate slowly, and when there's time to sit down, you ask which piece is still vibrating, still alive. How much do you write versus throw away? Her answer is one word: Most. A serious writer throws away many times what they keep, and that takes a little courage, to keep writing even when it's wrong. What really excites her is the editing stage, because ‘the beast is there’, the outline is already visible.

1:02:17 The cost of college is a problem, learning is not
She directly rebuts the claim that the humanities have no prospects: critical thinking, close reading, extracting meaning from complex texts, communicating persuasively, imagining other people's lives, understanding multiple cultures — these are capacities useful in any career. She doesn't deny that the cost of higher education is a real problem that really needs solving, but she puts the emphasis elsewhere: what's more worrying is the attack on the university itself, interference in its mission, and the loud repetition of the claim that ‘the university is not a valuable thing.’ Her last line is sharp: creating an undereducated populace serves another purpose.

1:07:22 Those who cannot read are the easiest to control
‘free people read freely’ is a line from the poet and librarian Tracie D. Hall, and Alexander says she borrows it all day long. She reads those five words from the African American tradition: under slavery, it was a crime for Black people to learn to read and write, and a crime for a free white person to teach them — what was being controlled was not words but people. So the line holds two halves: free people read freely, and, free people are meant to read. If a person cannot read, cannot access a mass of information, they cannot understand their own life, and so lose the capacity to act on an understanding of how outside forces work on them. Where literacy is stripped away, there is only one logic: this is how you are controlled.

item.title: Literacy Once Democratised Europe; Now It Is Going Backwards
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-econtalk-识字率曾让欧洲民主化-如今却在倒退/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-econtalk-识字率曾让欧洲民主化-如今却在倒退/
item.description: Writing cooled human communication from an emotional, face-to-face oral culture into a textual culture of evidence and logic; rising literacy once drove democratic revolutions, and screens are dragging public discourse back to a pre-literate age.
item.content:encoded:
Writing cooled human communication from an emotional, face-to-face oral culture into a textual culture of evidence and logic; rising literacy once drove democratic revolutions, and screens are dragging public discourse back to a pre-literate age.

Medium information density, but two mechanisms are worth hearing: "writing cools discourse" and "bad ideas are easier to whitewash on film"; the later section on pop music and reading is looser.

8:13 Literacy is historically very recent and very fragile
Marriott stresses that we are so used to literacy that we forget how anomalous it is. By one estimate, in a certain ancient Mesopotamian city-state there may have been only 20 living people who could read and write; literacy in ancient Rome was around 10%. For thousands of years, reading and writing was not a cultural phenomenon but an esoteric code circulating within a wealthy scribal elite — some rulers were literate, some were not. The real turning point was printing: books could be reproduced in quantity, more people could read them, and books became more practical; Protestantism then placed extreme emphasis on the written word, pushing more people to become literate in order to read the Bible. These factors fed each other until the "Reading Revolution" historians identify in the mid-to-late 18th century.

11:19 The Reading Revolution really did change political forms
Roberts pushes back: if literacy exploded, why doesn't the world look turned upside down? Marriott's answer is that the spread of literacy has a democratising effect — the more people who can access information and ideas, the more people participate in politics and criticise power. Early 18th-century Europe was ruled by absolute monarchs, and political affairs were essentially court secrets discussed among a small elite; by the late 18th and early 19th centuries, newspapers appeared, the standing of absolute monarchs declined sharply, France became a republic, the authority of the British monarch was far weaker than at the start of the century, parliamentary debates were reported, and public affairs were no longer discussed only in court. He calls this the great age of democratic revolution and democratic reform, and ties it directly to the spread of literacy.

16:32 Writing forces bad ideas into logical form
Marriott concedes that books are imperfect, but argues that the way books organise information is more rational and more coherent than conversation, video or TikTok. Writing forces you to polish an idea repeatedly, externalising part of your mind onto the page and then testing it; the reader faces a fixed text and can reread and analyse it critically. More crucially, books restrict the means of non-logical persuasion — you cannot bypass argument with charisma, shouting or tears. He uses the Nazis as a counterexample: Hitler's Mein Kampf was unreadable even to senior Nazis, because Nazism simply does not hold together once it is required to be presented coherently as a written text; Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will, by contrast, is treated as an artistic masterpiece, screened in film classes, and regarded as an extremely powerful argument for fascism. Bad ideas are easier to whitewash on a screen than in a book.

25:05 The Republic of Letters filtered out trolls by writing
The 17th- and 18th-century European "Republic of Letters" was a community of thinkers, philosophers and scientists who wrote to each other and ran journals. The economic historian Joel Mokyr rates it extraordinarily highly, even calling it the single cultural fact that explains the Industrial Revolution. Marriott's mechanism is this: if clever people sit alone in a village, their ideas can only be told to their neighbours, and scientific innovation struggles to accumulate; the spread of literacy let ideas travel further, more and more people joined the conversation, ideas flowed into one central pool, and thought became more and more complex. Roberts adds that the key difference is not public versus private but who the participants are — in conversation with Adam Smith, David Hume and Newton, the standard is naturally high; it is a kind of "submission to that which cannot be enforced". Marriott concedes that the literacy barrier itself carries a benign elitism: you cannot barge in and shout like a troll on X, because nobody will engage with you.

34:49 The novel gives us a passage into other minds
Marriott argues there is a kind of truth about life that only prose fiction can reach: it lets us see the inside of other people's minds. Reading is an active rather than passive process — you use the words on the page to build images in your head, which is why it is immersive, why it feels like having lived another life. Film cannot do this, because it gives you the external world and cannot enter another mind directly; writing, meanwhile, is precisely the medium we use to express what is in our minds, mind communicating with mind. He also notes that oral poetry has little interest in the subtle differences between human consciousnesses, and that this capacity to "inhabit another mind" appears only in prose fiction. Roberts does not fully agree, arguing that great films can get close through dialogue, but concedes that film almost never captures the inner activity that is conveyed by more than dialogue.

47:59 The post-literate commentator is more like Homer
Marriott writes that the post-literate commentator does not explain and analyse the world like the print-era public intellectual, but is more like an oral storyteller, weaving strange and unforgettable stories for a fascinated audience. Roberts calls this the deepest insight in the whole piece: faced with the mass of absurd, untenable statements online, people habitually interrogate them by the author's standard — "that isn't logical", "where's the evidence?" — but these people are simply not in that business. Their job is to entertain the audience; truth does not matter, what matters is a story that fascinates. Marriott goes further: presenting an argument logically, supplying evidence, driving to a rational conclusion — these are not in fact natural to human communication; in an oral culture, the more effective way to persuade someone is to entertain him, move him, get angry at him. Writing imposes an impersonal, more rational form of communication, and it is not a necessary product of human communication.

53:59 The richness of pop music also feeds on reading
Roberts cites an example from The History of Rock and Roll in 500 Songs: Jagger wrote "Sympathy for the Devil", whose opening is taken directly from Bulgakov's The Master and Margarita — the novel opens with two Russian intellectuals mocking God and faith, after which a suave gentleman appears, they think he is mad, and finally they realise it is Satan. Marriott calls this an "annoyingly good" example and regrets not putting it in the book. He concedes it cannot be pushed too far — it is not that you have to move Penguin Classics into the British Library to join a boy band — but Bob Dylan and Paul McCartney are both obviously heavy readers. He cites research showing that over the past 20 years pop songs have become less complex in both lyrics and melody, partly because the environment favours simplicity and immediacy: to go viral on TikTok, a song has to grab you within three or four seconds.

58:17 The future of reading will be deliberate, like fitness
Marriott stresses this is not a new phenomenon: statistics on the decline of serious reading go back to the 1950s and 1960s, television was the beginning of the screen age, and the remote control was the original doomscroll. Roberts quotes what his father said at the time — books have existed for centuries, television has been a mass medium for only 20 years, let's see if it lasts — and concedes his father should have worried more. Marriott's consolation comes from an analogy with junk food and fitness: McDonald's arrived, many people got fat, but some realised that health could no longer be absorbed naturally from the environment and required deliberate effort, so they started running and going to the gym. He guesses cognitive health will follow the same path: if reading has a future, it will become more deliberate, less "I'm bored at the airport, I'll pick up a book" and more "I value this experience, so I sit down and read for half an hour to an hour every night". He admits this makes him a little sad, because reading will become more artificial, no longer the unavoidable part of life it once was.

item.title: A Glass of Water Has No Final Truth: Quantum Mechanics Forces Us to Give Up the Single Perspective
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-startweek-一杯水没有终极真相-量子力学逼我们放弃单一视角/

item.description: Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not a new particle, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is many perspectives that enrich one another but never converge.
item.content:encoded:
Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not a new particle, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is many perspectives that enrich one another but never converge.

A four-person roundtable crossing physics, poetry, drama and economics; high density of quotable lines but the argument wanders. Worth listening if you want a few perspectives that can change your judgment; skip it if you want hard information.

2:06 A glass of water has no final version
Rovelli opens with a glass of water that the BBC provided: you look from one side, I look from the other, you wear glasses and I see a different colour. This glass of water can be a physical object (mass, velocity, position), it can be temperature and pressure, it can be the chemistry of H2O plus floating bits, it can be the global economy of being bottled in Italy and shipped to England, or it can simply be "we want to drink it." His claim is that all these perspectives are real, none exhausts another, none contradicts another, and there is no "ultimate glass of water." This is anti-Platonic — he does not accept a distinction between a "level of appearances" and a "fundamental level."

6:13 We have not yet digested quantum mechanics
Rovelli says what he is describing is not borrowed from philosophy but grown from inside physics. Physicists ran into quantum phenomena; quantum mechanics is an enormous revolution, but "we have not yet digested quantum mechanics" — the newspaper stories about experiments that "confirm what I learned in a textbook in the 1970s" show precisely that we do not yet truly believe it. Take quantum mechanics seriously and what it says is this: the Enlightenment dream of "describing reality completely, determinately, clearly, independently of the observer" does not hold. The observer here need not be a human; anything that interacts with something else counts.

8:19 The deepest level of reality is not more objective
Rovelli turns it around: the most basic level of reality physics can reach is in fact not essentially different from the reality Lavinia deals with in poetry, or the characters in James's play deal with in economics — both are realities that allow different views, not a reality that is "absolutely objective underneath." So quantum physics is not that hard; it simply has not been digested. The concrete physical phenomena are of course very complex, but poetry is complex and economics is complex too.

10:25 Scientists have always used metaphors
Rovelli says the words Lavinia uses could be lifted line by line into his book. What is an electron? "It is a grain, a grain of sand, but it is not really a grain of sand." Why is an electric field called a field? Because it is "a bit like a field in the countryside." We think through metaphors, by taking old concepts apart and piecing together a new concept from a bit of each. The goal is not to arrive at a final, perfect description of reality — a century ago we thought we could, but it does not work — but to gain a better understanding, a better way of navigating reality. He adds a crucial qualification: admitting that everything has a perspective does not mean all perspectives are equivalent, nor that there is no better and worse; it is only that the hope of "arriving at the final correct story about reality" is empty — not unreachable, but meaningless.

12:27 Seeking an ultimate morality is itself wrong
Rovelli turns from "complexity" to "value": if you ask "what is the ultimate definition of good and evil, what is universal ethics," he thinks this is itself a morally and ethically wrong approach. Our morals and values are powerful, important and indispensable not because they are outside us, but because they are inside us, and therefore equally perspectival. This passage connects directly to James Graham's play — whose first line is "what is a good life."

15:30 Do not be afraid to learn a jargon
Lavinia Greenlaw argues for embracing jargon: not everyone has to learn it, but if you are genuinely interested in something, do not be afraid to learn its language — a mechanic has to learn the names of parts, a surgeon has to learn the names of parts, and a poet has to as well. It lets you see more clearly, and it lets you see where something has gone wrong. She admits jargon can be exclusionary, but "that depends on the context in which you use it," and "you can perform difficulty, and poets and poems are probably quite good at that, but that is not what difficulty means." She gives the example of poems on the underground: before everyone looked at their phones, people would read a poem first and only then realise it was a poem, and that engagement was far more direct and confident than sitting down and being told "now you are going to read a poem."

22:55 Friction is treated as a problem to be solved
James Graham says modern culture has fetishised "efficiency" and stripped out every layer of difficulty as friction. He gives a concrete image: emailing himself a script to save it, a prompt pops up — "this is a long document, shall I summarise it for you?" — and his reaction is "how rude, I want you to sit inside it and read it." He connects this back to Bloomsbury and Keynes: meaning is found precisely in the friction, in the difficulty, in the process. He also says the collapse of reading is despairing, because reading demands personal investment, and today that investment is treated as a problem to be solved rather than something to be celebrated.

26:05 War refuses to acknowledge complexity
Rovelli uses International Peace Day on 21 September, and remarks by the UN Secretary-General and the Pope, to connect the perspectival argument to war: war is to a large extent driven by greed and power games, but it always wraps itself in a hypocritical narrative — there is only one truth, only one good, we are the good ones, they are the bad ones, we tell the truth, they tell lies and propaganda. So war is built on a total refusal to be prepared to accept complexity, perspectives, and worldviews different from our own. The host, Adam Rutherford, offers a counterexample on the spot: we also always need to seek simplicity, and if you embraced difficulty and acted the scholar all day you might get nothing done and enjoy nothing. Lavinia's response pulls the topic back to rhetoric: language therefore matters more than ever, and poetry and poetics can teach people to argue.

item.description: Ternus's debut was about an intelligent personal hub, but the event introduced no new AI features; Apple's AI is propped up by Google's models, while its real bet is on a foldable and a pile of product categories that don't exist yet.
item.content:encoded:
Ternus's debut was about an intelligent personal hub, but the event introduced no new AI features; Apple's AI is propped up by Google's models, while its real bet is on a foldable and a pile of product categories that don't exist yet.

Mark Gurman is the most accurate reporter on Apple, and this episode strings executive turnover, the AI roadmap, the privacy controversy and foldable predictions into one line, with high information density.

5:09 The biggest difference between Ternus and Cook is that he'll make the call
Gurman says the event was almost interchangeable with the Cook era, with the only difference being that Ternus opened by laying out a view on AI. The mechanism he gives is management style: you bring an idea to Cook and he keeps probing with questions, in many cases not making a single decision — it's collective decision-making; you go to Ternus and he gives you a decision, gives you an opinion, you may hate the opinion, but he takes a position. Gurman stresses this is exactly the biggest difference between the two men from talking to insiders, and it explains why Ternus talked about AI first thing on stage.

8:20 The 2026 event had not one new AI feature
Gurman points out that Apple held a big product event in September 2026 but rolled out no notable new AI features, and the roughly 15-minute opening just retold the Apple Intelligence story of the past two years. His explanation: Apple has gone as far on AI as it can and can only tell the best story with the cards it holds; and Apple has no AI-centric device, so it has to prop up the iPhone as its AI device until a killer device appears and it can switch narratives.

13:29 Under Cook, Apple became an institution
Gurman draws a distinction between the Cook era and the Jobs era: in the Cook era people's relationship with Apple is a relationship with an institution — global, enormous, like IBM; the Jobs era was one new product after another redefining a category. He also corrects the host's read on Vision Pro — every time he writes that Vision Pro is on life support, he gets dozens of reactions close to death-threat level, because some people have built businesses around spatial computing and some consumers paid four thousand dollars for it.

20:45 Apple spent five years swapping out the old guard one by one
Gurman reconstructs the rhythm of the handover: in 2023 Cook began saying at every executive meeting that succession had to be taken seriously; at the time the top ranks either had five hundred million in the bank or were billionaires, and were close in age. So they lined up the order and went one by one — at the end of 2024 CFO Luca Maestri retired, replaced by Kevin Parekh; in 2025 COO Jeff Williams retired, succeeded by his deputy; in 2026 the general counsel changed, with Jennifer Newstead poached from Meta; and only at the end of 2026 did Cook hand the baton to Ternus. Gurman calls this retention strategy Hotel California: you never want to leave.

28:07 The chip chief was kept with a title invented on the spot
Gurman says the second most important person at Apple now is the hardware head, who built Apple Silicon, Apple's key differentiator. In late summer or early autumn last year he went to tell Cook he was quitting, right in the middle of preparations for Ternus to take over. Cook had him stay to take part in the transition and promised him the title of chief hardware officer, which Apple had never had, letting him keep his existing team and also take over Ternus's side of the business. Gurman judges this is not a long-term arrangement and that the man already wants to leave again — he conquered the Mac, shed Intel and Qualcomm, and Apple has no next goal for him; he may leave within a year or two, and then the hardware engineering team will have to be split apart again, because no successor carries his industry weight.

33:15 Willing to spend tens of billions on a modem, yet says it needn't own AI
What Gurman finds most absurd is executives saying in interviews over the past year that ‘we never owned search, we don't need to own AI’. He counters: these are two completely different things, and Apple spent tens of billions to own a cellular modem that had already been commoditised, buying and fixing Intel's modem business — willing to do that for a modem but unwilling to own AI is ridiculous. The internal idea was originally to partner with Google as a stopgap until it could build its own models, but Gurman says he has seen no evidence that Apple is pushing its own models again, making big AI acquisitions, or paying AI researchers top salaries.

48:53 The watch's always-on transcription stepped on the privacy landmine
Gurman's reaction to the Apple Watch's always-listening feature was ‘I can't believe they did it’. The feature only transcribes, doesn't record or store, and a double tap shows you the last 15 seconds of what someone said to you, without their consent. He says Apple knows the next-generation interface needs some degree of ambient capture, but the societal privacy problem is unsolved: technical white papers, private cloud compute and encryption can't hold back the social backlash. He thinks Apple could have put audio and visual intelligence together next year and told one coherent privacy story; as it is, it's boiling the frog slowly.

57:05 Foldables will become the new normal within a decade
Gurman offers a bold prediction: foldables will become the new normal within a decade. He draws an analogy with smartphone penetration — at the end of 2006 smartphones were about 6% of the market, now they're 85%, and they crossed the halfway mark five or six years later; the iPhone itself wasn't the source of that, but it pulled everyone into the smartphone game, and he thinks the iPhone Duo will do the same for the phone market. He also mentions the iPhone's number migration feature, hinting at a future combination of a foldable for work and a smaller, lighter phone for weekends with family.
