In 2006 most people didn't have smartphones; FedEx, UPS and Amazon could track packages, but on a scale of days, not minutes. Real-time tracking of pizza progress was entirely new. The designer's interface looked like a horizontal thermometer: order, prep, bake, box, deliver — each step completed, the next segment turned red. When David saw the mockup he said: "That's a hot dog. We're a pizza company, why is there a hot dog?" But executives liked it, and decided to launch before the Super Bowl.

15:36 Designers use the pizza tracker as a meeting prop
Shuya Gong was a design director at IDEO and later taught design at Harvard. Consulting for many companies in the mid-2010s, she found one of the most effective ways to open a meeting was to order a pizza on the spot, throw the tracker up on the big screen, and ask the client: "How do you feel right now?" She says you can feel the anxiety rise or fall in your body, feel the reassurance and groundedness. Then you can ask: which of those parts do you want your users to feel when they use your product? The pizza tracker became shorthand in her design circle: whenever a client involved waiting, they'd say "they need a pizza tracker."

17:39 The tracker manufactures a labor illusion
Shuya says one reason the pizza tracker caught on is that as shopping became more digital, the tracker replicated something important from the physical world — watching other people work. Online experiences lack that visibility, so people get impatient more easily. Researchers found that reminding customers there's labor behind a product makes them value it more, and called it the "labor illusion." Shuya also describes a stranger mechanism: the tracker changes our perception of time. Like walking somewhere and feeling the return trip is shorter because it's familiar and has landmarks. The pizza tracker gives us a familiar route and landmarks — pizza being made, on the road, being delivered — making the wait feel shorter.

19:47 Banks deliberately slow transfers to fake a wait
Working with banks and fintech companies in the mid-2010s, Shuya found their problem was the opposite of Domino's: customers weren't used to transfers being so fast. Two computers talk, confirm the amount, and the money is gone — no road to cross, no cheese to melt. But for people used to money taking a while to arrive, instant arrival "feels suspicious." So companies deliberately slow down the "money tracker," giving you no real-time feedback but adding a buffer that makes you wait. Shuya says this is intentionally slowing time, adding meaningful friction so that in the wait you feel the seriousness and weight of the transfer. The host presses: isn't that advising lying to customers? Shuya says she'd rather understand it as "curating the experience," adding back the physicality that existed in the traditional experience, to make people comfortable.

21:48 TurboTax and Uber progress bars may be fake
TurboTax pops up animations during filing saying "we're checking your deductions and credits." But a few years ago someone looked at the code and found the animation was identical for everyone, in every situation, and took the same amount of time. The question is: is TurboTax trying to reassure us during the terrifying ordeal of filing taxes, or using the labor illusion to make us feel a big payment is worth it? Uber is similar: the host repeatedly got updated pickup times, but the car almost always arrived later than promised. It felt like the tracker was part of a deliberate deception — to make you choose Uber over Lyft, to keep you from cancelling, to get you standing on the street early. The show reached out to TurboTax and Uber; TurboTax didn't respond, Uber didn't arrange an interview but shared some data suggesting their pickup times are fairly accurate.

25:52 Field test: the pizza tracker is mostly real
Nick biked to a local Domino's to stake it out, while Alex ordered a half-Hawaiian, half-pepperoni pizza at home and monitored the tracker in real time. Nick ordered a pepperoni pizza in the store as cover. The tracker showed "Ivan" making the pizza, but when Nick asked the staff their name, they said "Alex." The tracker also showed a "quality check," but Nick saw no quality inspector. David had explained, though, that because Domino's uses conveyor ovens, the bake time is nearly fixed, so the tracker automatically jumps to the next step after a set time. Eventually the pizza came out, was boxed, and was driven off by Alex (aka Ivan), with Nick chasing on his bike and nearly being taken for a stalker. Alex hit "delivered" at Nick's door and the tracker updated quickly. Conclusion: the tracker is mostly accurate, but "Ivan is making it" and the "quality check" are fake.

item.title: AI Proves in Half an Hour a Math Theorem Humans Couldn't Crack in a Year
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-instituteforad-ai-半小时证出人类一年没做出的数学定理/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-instituteforad-ai-半小时证出人类一年没做出的数学定理/
item.description: A stuck L^p problem, a five-page proof from AI in half an hour, a 60-page paper compressed to its core lemma, and the threshold for continuous density pushed from 588 down to 9.
item.content:encoded:
A stuck L^p problem, a five-page proof from AI in half an hour, a 60-page paper compressed to its core lemma, and the threshold for continuous density pushed from 588 down to 9.

If you care about what AI can actually do in pure mathematics, this episode gives a concrete, verifiable case: not assisting with computation, but supplying a proof structure no human had thought of.

0:18 For the first time, AI had a good idea
The speaker says this is the first time he has encountered a model that "really had a good idea" on a problem he had worked on for a long time, and that the idea led to "very elegant efficient progress." Note his wording: it is not that AI helped him compute, it is that AI supplied a proof approach he had not thought of. He credits the result to Astra and says it was done only last week.

8:13 The key theorem: absolute continuity automatically carries L^p
The core theorem is: if a self-similar measure μ is absolutely continuous, then its density automatically lies in some L^p with p greater than 1. What actually excites the speaker is not the fact itself but that p is quantitative — p can be expressed explicitly in terms of the mass μ gives to small balls. Because p is quantitative, one can bring over methods for studying explicit absolute continuity, construct explicit L^p examples, and from there get continuous density.

12:27 p can never be made uniform
The speaker specifically warns: p can never be made uniform. For any dimension d and any p greater than 1, there exists some self-similar measure that lies in L^1 but not in L^p. So this quantitative result must not be read as "all absolutely continuous self-similar measures have uniform L^p integrability" — it is a case-by-case bound that depends on the mass distribution.

23:45 Splitting λ into odd and even parts
The trick for proving continuous density: split the random series of the Bernoulli convolution into odd and even terms; after factoring a λ out of the odd part, what remains is exactly the even part. So μ_λ equals μ_{λ²} convolved with itself. If λ² falls in the range where Solomyak proved L^2 holds almost surely, then the convolution of two L^2 functions is continuous, and μ_λ has continuous density. This is the bridge from an L^2 result to continuity.

34:17 A 60-page paper compressed into 5 pages
The speaker says the core idea was in fact already his and his collaborator's, but that AI was "extremely elegant and efficient" in using it. Varju's paper is 60 pages, his own is also very long, and AI compressed the step from one result to another into 5 pages; and after "maybe a bit of a weakening," another 5 pages suffice to get a stronger conclusion. He stresses this is not AI thinking up the core idea for him, it is AI combining known tools in a way he "could have never" done.

36:18 Half an hour to run, 50 hours to formalise
Asked about runtime, the speaker says "not long, maybe half an hour." The whole result was then formalised in Lean, which took about 50 hours. He also mentions tricks like a goal command that let the model "really try hard." The comparison: it might have taken him a year, and "if you sent me this paper to referee, I would like who is this person?"

39:21 The continuous-density threshold drops from 588 to 9
For the case λ = 1 - 1/n, AI proves μ_λ is continuous when n is greater than 588 — the speaker says this is not yet the result of him pushing the constant, "if I push the constant, I could easily push the constant more." Even more striking is another result: absolute continuity when n is greater than 9, which the speaker says "I could not dare think I could prove"; he himself pushed for two and a half hours to get to 9, while the ideal target is 3.

43:23 The key lemma comes from an obscure paper
At the heart of the proof is a lemma from geometric measure theory: for a positive L^1 function f, if the mass of a set inside a small ball is small and the integral of f over that set is also small, then f lies in some explicit L^p, with p given explicitly by C, ε, and A. The speaker says the lemma is "not too difficult to prove," about a page, but "extremely difficult to find because it's not a very well-known fact" — it was dug out of some random papers.

item.title: Looney Tunes animator Chuck Jones: A character isn't drawn, it's thought up
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freshair-乐一通-动画师-角色不是画出来的-是想出来的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freshair-乐一通-动画师-角色不是画出来的-是想出来的/
item.description: Chuck Jones said the key to animation isn't what a character looks like or how it's drawn, but "who he is" — he understood the character first, which is how Daffy could be cowardly and overbearing at once, and how Bugs Bunny could only fight back after being provoked.
item.content:encoded:
Chuck Jones said the key to animation isn't what a character looks like or how it's drawn, but "who he is" — he understood the character first, which is how Daffy could be cowardly and overbearing at once, and how Bugs Bunny could only fight back after being provoked.

The first half, the Chuck Jones interview, is information-dense; the second half, the Cassandra Wilson segment, is mostly music appreciation, so you can listen to just the interview portion.

0:00 Bugs Bunny's violence wouldn't pass review today
Comedian Dustin Nickerson tried showing classic cartoons to his young daughter and found they hadn't become harmless with time: plenty of characters have speech impediments, and the behavior is highly aggressive. Pepe Le Pew forcibly holds a female character so she can't leave, while other characters murder each other — the Coyote wants to kill the bird. This runs counter to the cartoon impression in viewers' memories that "everyone is friends."

4:04 A shelved Warner film was saved by an independent distributor
After Coyote vs. Acme was finished, Warner Bros. Discovery shelved it and wrote it off financially. This year an independent distributor bought the rights for $50 million, and last month it finally opened. The film played in relatively few theaters across the U.S., but it has already recouped almost its entire cost domestically, with another $30 million overseas. The movie itself is about the Coyote suing the Acme Corporation, inspired by Ian Frazier's 1990 parody piece in The New Yorker.

7:07 Daffy is cowardly and overbearing at the same time
Chuck Jones said what makes Daffy funny is that he rushes in and is afraid to take a step at the same time, is sycophantic and domineering at the same time — like when we go into the boss's office to ask for a raise, domineering on the way in, sycophantic once inside, except Daffy does both simultaneously. He admitted he couldn't understand "crazy" characters, so he always had to "pasteurize" a character and figure out who he is. He stressed that the point of character animation isn't what the character looks like, nor how it's drawn, but "who he is."

9:11 Bugs Bunny is a comedy hero, not a comedy loser
Jones first did Duck Amuck with Daffy, then later did Rabbit Rampage with Bugs Bunny, and the same setup didn't hold, because Bugs isn't that kind of character. He classified Bugs as a comedy hero, whereas the lineage of Chaplin and Buster Keaton are all half-losers, more like ordinary people. He liked Daffy because Daffy keeps going, right to the point where Jones himself would stop for fear of what others would think.

10:14 A two-hour "yes session" where no one may say anything negative
After 1946, Warner's cartoons were directed by three men: Fritz Freeling, Bob McKimpson and Jones. Whoever had an idea for a film called the other directors and the writers into a meeting they called a "yes session": for two hours no one was allowed to say anything negative, and if you had nothing to contribute you shut up. The result was that everyone participated in everyone else's films, but each director had absolute control over the content of his own, with no infighting among them. Jones also admitted that if a good gag he'd given was used by Freeling and the audience laughed, he naturally wanted to go throw up — that's human nature, and it was the Daffy in him.

13:25 The narrower the rules, the better the comedy
Jones believed that in comedy, the more you narrow and restrict a character, the better it works: once Chaplin put on the Little Tramp outfit, what he could do was locked down. Once Roadrunner and Coyote were fixed in the American Southwest desert, the rules followed — Roadrunner has to stay on the road, can never hurt Coyote, and Coyote can only hurt himself through the unlucky Acme products he buys, with no sound in the whole film except "beep-beep." Bugs Bunny is too strong and easily becomes a bully, so every film first lets him live his own life in his natural rabbit environment until someone comes to take his hide or his life, and only then does he fight back.

16:30 Hiding one dirty frame in a twenty-fourth of a second
Jones admitted that Warner's animators all drew that kind of pornographic cartoon on the sly. He himself would sometimes slip a single frame — a twenty-fourth of a second — of a dirty image into a Pepe Le Pew film, then call the office manager over and say there seemed to be a little glitch here that he couldn't figure out. He knew no one could see it, but the manager would be shocked on the spot. He always kept a replacement frame on hand just in case, but he enjoyed doing it, in his words, to "reduce him to moccasins."

17:31 The networks cut films until they were incomprehensible
Jones said his scenes and lines were never censored; that was left to the "brilliant people" at the networks, and what they cut made the whole film incomprehensible. Both CBS and ABC did it. What he found absurd was that the Roadrunner series, the one most complained about for violence, actually has no violence — Roadrunner never hurts Coyote, and Coyote is simply the victim of his own incompetence.

item.title: The last IMO problem AI could not solve — and why the answer isn't the point
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-karpathy-ai-解不出的最后一道-imo-题-价值不在答案/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-karpathy-ai-解不出的最后一道-imo-题-价值不在答案/
item.description: In 2025, fewer than 1% of IMO contestants scored full marks on Problem 6, and every AI got stuck on it. What makes it hard isn't computation — it's that you have to understand first, have taste first, and only then start writing. And that is exactly what reinforcement learning struggles most to train.
item.content:encoded:
In 2025, fewer than 1% of IMO contestants scored full marks on Problem 6, and every AI got stuck on it. What makes it hard isn't computation — it's that you have to understand first, have taste first, and only then start writing. And that is exactly what reinforcement learning struggles most to train.

The bulk of this episode is a complete walkthrough of one math problem, not AI industry analysis. Only the last 5 minutes discuss the relationship between AI and math, but those 5 minutes are worth hearing.

0:00 What blocks AI isn't computation, it's patience
On 2025 IMO Problem 6, of more than 600 top contestants worldwide, fewer than 1% scored full marks. By 2025, models from several institutions could answer every other problem correctly, and got stuck only on this one. DeepMind research director Thang Luong's explanation: the model has no patience — it won't spend time understanding the problem or developing a feel for it, it just starts solving. Karpathy adds a second reason: the model has no sense of what makes a problem or a strategy beautiful, and this problem's solution depends precisely on aesthetic judgment.

6:11 Genius is really the residue of experience
Facing this problem, the most obvious construction is to put all the X's on the diagonal, cover the remaining region with horizontal tiles, and get 2(n-1) tiles. But that construction is too obvious to be the answer IMO wants. Karpathy inserts a seemingly unrelated cube-cutting brainteaser here: a 3x3x3 cube cut into 27 small cubes, where you're allowed to rearrange the pieces after each cut — what's the minimum number of cuts? The answer is 6, because each of the 6 faces of the very center cube needs its own separate cut. That proof idea — fix your attention on one face of the internal structure — is exactly the key to the tiling problem later.

12:17 The most efficient tiling has every tile touching four X's
Highlight all four edges of every X, and each time you place a tile, switch off the edges it touches. In an inefficient tiling, a tile touches only 1 or even 0 X's; in an efficient tiling, every tile touches 4 X's. This yields a conjecture: the optimal tiling should make as many tiles as possible touch 4 distinct X's. But look further: an X cannot sit in the middle of a tile's edge — that would make the two tiles above and below conflict on the left, since a column can't contain two X's. The X must sit at a corner of tiles, with four tiles pinwheeling around it. With square tiles of side length k, you can tile a large grid of side length k². 2025 happens to be 45², and this coincidence makes the construction look extremely promising.

19:27 Highlight only one direction and the proof misses the tiles on one side
Highlight the edges of all X's: 4k² edges in total, each tile touches at most 4, subtract the 4 on the boundary that don't need to be touched, and you get the lower bound k²-1. But the target lower bound is k²+2k-3, off by a term proportional to k. The problem is highlighting only the right edge: the correspondence you get this way is tight on the right side of the diagram, but misses a large number of tiles concentrated on the left. Switching to any other single direction is the same — the missed tiles always cluster on one side. Karpathy says math rewards you for respecting symmetry and punishes you for not respecting it — pick an arbitrary direction and the weakness shows up in the inequality.

27:38 Cut the grid into four regions, highlight each edge only once
The solution is to draw two paths: one going up-right along the X's, one going down-right, dividing the whole diagram into four regions. If an X is in the right region, highlight its right edge; if in the top region, highlight its top edge — left, right, top, bottom each govern one region. An X lying on a boundary highlights two edges. This both fills in the missing highlighted edges and guarantees that every tile touches at most one highlighted edge — because when a tile sits in the left region, the X above it cannot highlight a bottom edge, the X below it cannot highlight a top edge, and the X to its left cannot highlight a right edge. This diagram is the core of the entire proof.

31:48 The problem reduces to a pure permutation problem
Label each X with its row number; since each row has exactly one X, these labels form a permutation of 1 to k². The up-right path corresponds to an increasing subsequence, the down-right path to a decreasing subsequence. Let LIS be the length of the longest increasing subsequence and LDS the longest decreasing subsequence; the total number of highlighted edges is k² + LIS + LDS - 4 (or -3 when the two paths intersect, adding 1 back). To prove the target lower bound k²+2k-3, it suffices to prove LIS + LDS ≥ 2k, i.e. that the average of the two is at least k. At this point the grid has completely vanished, and what remains is a pure fact about permutations.

39:59 The proof of Erdős-Szekeres is itself a gem
This pure permutation fact is the Erdős-Szekeres theorem: in any permutation, the product of the lengths of the longest increasing subsequence and the longest decreasing subsequence is at least the length n of the permutation. An IMO contestant could just cite the theorem and finish, but Karpathy chooses to give the proof too. The approach is to label each position with a pair of numbers: the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending there, and the length of the longest decreasing subsequence ending there. Because the numbers in a permutation are all distinct, the two label pairs at any two positions must differ — if the later number is larger, the first label increases by at least one; if smaller, the second label increases by at least one. Plot these label pairs as coordinate points: the longest increasing subsequence is the width of the bounding box, the longest decreasing subsequence is the height, and width times height equals the number of lattice points, which is the length of the permutation.

48:08 Beyond the proof there's another layer: making the proof feel obvious
Karpathy says knowing a proof is only a very small part of deeply understanding mathematics. When he and Nishad Dulkhar made this video, their first reaction on seeing the original proof was ‘I know it's true, but how would anyone come up with this’. What they wanted to contribute wasn't a new proof but a narrative, so that when viewers reach the proof it no longer feels like it appeared out of nowhere. He has a name for this: motivated explanation. This bears directly on AI and math: if a machine can generate proofs but doesn't bring human understanding, then it has completely lost its meaning. And academia has long used ‘proof’ as a proxy metric for progress, which exposes an urgent need — for a new, independent way to measure whether a publication actually advances human understanding.

item.title: NASA Administrator: We Are Not a Procurement Agency, We Are a Nuclear-Powered NASA
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-allin-nasa-局长-我们不是采购机构-是核动力-nasa/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-allin-nasa-局长-我们不是采购机构-是核动力-nasa/
item.description: Jared Isaacman says NASA used to spread resources across every congressional district and partner for partnership's sake, and the result is a lunar rocket less efficient than the Saturn V; what he wants to build is nuclear power and nuclear propulsion, and to hand low Earth orbit to companies like SpaceX.
item.content:encoded:
Jared Isaacman says NASA used to spread resources across every congressional district and partner for partnership's sake, and the result is a lunar rocket less efficient than the Saturn V; what he wants to build is nuclear power and nuclear propulsion, and to hand low Earth orbit to companies like SpaceX.

This is the policy manifesto of NASA's new administrator, with information density concentrated on the lunar south pole, nuclear power and the Mars plan, though the back half of the interview is soft and the Q&A quality is middling.

2:06 NASA used to spread resources thin to please everyone
Isaacman sorts NASA's problems into two categories: externally imposed and self-inflicted. Partnering for partnership's sake turned partnerships into a drag on missions rather than an accelerator. The result is that Orion cannot inject into low lunar orbit the way Apollo did; the previous administration cancelled Mars Sample Return because the cost would exceed an aircraft carrier. He also says NASA built programs that are "too big to fail and too expensive to ever really succeed," betting they would survive across administrations. Core capabilities were rented out, outsourced or simply lost, and progress that should have taken months turned into years at greatly increased cost.

3:07 The lunar rocket is less efficient than the Saturn V of sixty years ago
He offers a jarring comparison: China's rockets were designed when locomotives still burned coal, and today China operates 25,000 miles of high-speed rail and is only a few years from its own Apollo 11 moment. Meanwhile NASA's lunar rocket is less efficient than the Saturn V at converting launch mass into payload headed to the Moon; the gap between Artemis 1 and Artemis 2 is longer than all 12 Gemini missions of sixty years ago combined. The lunar space station puts astronauts in a position to look down on the most coveted lunar real estate rather than working on the surface and occupying it.

7:07 The lunar south pole has only a few good parking spots
The Moon's surface area is roughly that of Africa, but the south pole is only about the size of Washington, D.C., and the usable permanently shadowed craters are limited. Those craters hold water ice, and the environment is harsher than Mars itself; the crater walls in turn offer near-permanent solar illumination. So good landing sites are very few. He notes that a Starship-sized vehicle landing on the lunar surface will blast out a crater and throw debris, further shrinking the usable spots. China's robotic mission is targeting Shackleton Crater next year, and China and Russia are also cooperating on a nuclear-powered lunar base.

8:07 A 100-kilowatt fission reactor launches in 2028
NASA is saying goodbye to failed nuclear programs that have not left the lab since 1965, and in 2028 it will launch SR1 Freedom, a 100-kilowatt fission reactor. The mission will fly past Mars and release Skyfall, carrying three Ingenuity-class helicopters and using ground-penetrating radar to scout subsurface ice and future landing sites. He calls this the beginning of a "nuclear-powered NASA," turning its workforce and facilities back toward doing nearly impossible missions with no obvious commercial case. SR2, SR3 and SR4 follow, with targets including Enceladus, Europa and Titan, moons with oceans and complex chemistry.

23:22 The hardest part of Mars is not getting there, it is coming back
Pure chemical propulsion can put astronauts on Mars too, at speeds comparable to going to the Moon, and the habitation problem was solved long ago. The hard part is how to come back: you need to manufacture propellant on the Martian surface, and the plan is robots plus football-field-sized solar arrays, with the dust from sandstorms periodically blown off. He says doing this at one atmosphere and 1G on Earth is already extremely difficult. NASA's answer is to stop doing what industry already does well and turn to next-generation capabilities with no commercial case: fission power, plus a chemically enhanced nuclear transfer vehicle using krypton or xenon rather than manufacturing propellant on the Martian surface.

25:23 Hiring is not hard, retaining talent is
NASA's internship program accepts only 1% of applicants, so recruiting is not the early problem. The problem is whether it can keep people. If NASA does the same things as SpaceX, Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, Stoke and ULA while still flying fifty-year-old space shuttle hardware, it will lose talent. His approach: once a breakthrough has a commercial case, such as launch, NASA becomes one customer among many, hands the capability to industry and moves on to the next new thing. SR1 is only the start of a nuclear-powered NASA, their Nautilus, and a whole nuclear fleet will follow.

27:24 Nuclear propulsion is essentially an ion thruster in space
He explains the principle: the ion thrusters on Starlink satellites generate power from solar panels, ionize and accelerate krypton or xenon and expel it, giving extremely high exhaust velocity, very low thrust but very high efficiency, so propellant lasts a long time. The farther you get from the Sun, the more useless solar power becomes, and near Jupiter it is essentially negligible. At that point you switch to the heat of a nuclear reactor, starting at 100 kilowatts and possibly scaling to 250 kilowatts or even megawatts. The reactor should run as hot as possible, using high-temperature materials and a closed Brayton cycle to convert heat to electricity, then drive the same thrusters, just scaled up from 12, 14, 25 kilowatts.

28:24 NASA does not lack budget, it lacks capital allocation ability
He says NASA does not have a top line problem but has long been terrible at capital allocation, partly by NASA's own choice and partly imposed by others. The budget is now $25 billion. He asks how many founders are in the room and says $25 billion is a lot of money that can build pretty amazing hardware. In aeronautics, he complains that NASA's aviation budget is used to subsidize high-TRL programs at big contractors, such as a forty-year-old engine where NASA is asked to pay to squeeze out another 3% in fuel efficiency. He wants to get back to radical airframe and engine designs.

item.title: Wanting to Save the World Is No Excuse for a Monopoly Agreement
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-moneystuff-想拯救世界-不是搞垄断协议的借口/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-moneystuff-想拯救世界-不是搞垄断协议的借口/
item.description: AI labs want to jointly slow down model development, but four giants sitting down to talk about deceleration is, legally, a textbook antitrust conspiracy — wanting to save the world is not a defense.
item.content:encoded:
AI labs want to jointly slow down model development, but four giants sitting down to talk about deceleration is, legally, a textbook antitrust conspiracy — wanting to save the world is not a defense.

Three segments: the insider-trading evidentiary problem, Dario's deceleration memo, and pension privatization. Medium information density; the last two segments are worth more.

2:05 Suing a hundred John Does doesn't fly with the judge
Susquehanna spotted heavy buying of short-dated put options in Chinese brokerage stocks before cross-border trading was restricted, so it sued 100 John Does to freeze the accounts. But the judge denied the preliminary injunction: it could not be proven that all 100 were conspiring to trade on inside information. Levine's breakdown is that only a tiny few may have actually gotten the inside tip, while the rest just saw the tape move and piled in — and piling into publicly visible price moves is itself entirely legal. The party that can actually figure out who is who is the securities regulator, not the market maker that got picked off.

8:13 The market maker's losses may not be that big
Susquehanna claims it lost about $70 million on those puts, but Levine points out that is only half the story: as an options market maker, after selling puts it would normally hedge immediately, possibly by shorting the stock, or by buying puts back from another client or another market maker. If Citadel Securities and Susquehanna were both selling and both buying that day, they were effectively betting against each other and should in theory be suing each other. So the "lost $70 million" figure obscures the fact that they were also hedging, and may even have been net up on the day.

15:21 Not training new models is actually more profitable
Levine offers a counterintuitive business logic: model capability now runs ahead of deployment in many domains, and Anthropic and OpenAI are working with private equity firms to push AI into enterprises. If they stopped model development for a year, they could make a lot of money selling existing models, with quite good unit economics. But competitive pressure forces every frontier lab to keep burning huge sums training the next model — both to win customers on the leaderboard and to win researchers, because researchers want to go to the best lab. So "slowing down" is good for business, but no one dares unilaterally lay down the weapon.

19:25 Four of them sitting down to talk deceleration is collusion
Since no one dares slow down unilaterally, could the four frontier labs sit down and reach an agreement? Levine says that is legally a classic antitrust conspiracy — like the case in which BlackRock was sued by several state attorneys general: ESG investors got coal companies to produce less coal on the grounds that global warming is bad for humanity, but the effect was higher coal prices, making them the OPEC of coal. The line in the ruling is "wanting to save the world is no excuse for an antitrust conspiracy." Dario's memo also adds a footnote saying antitrust law would need to be appropriately amended before they would be allowed to sit in a room and discuss shutting down the killer robots.

22:28 The founding documents are all handwritten by humans
Sylvia read Kevin Roos's book on the AGI race (out October 6; she had a pre-read copy) and found a contrast: every dramatic turning point in the book corresponds to a human handwritten memo — Dario's Pacing the Frontier, the Say AGI memo, and so on. Yet what everyone discusses now is "was this written by AI." Reading Dario's memo, she instinctively wondered "did Claude write this," and concluded it did not read like AI at all — these people are philosophers writing original founding texts. But the next generation will probably just ask Claude what to do.

27:31 A 401k has no funding gap, only a balance that's too small
A pension is a future cash flow the company has promised, and the company must invest to match that liability; invest wrong and there is a funding gap, which is why ERISA steps in to govern pension insolvency. A 401k is not a promised cash flow, just a pool of money: if stocks fall, they fall, and there is no such thing on the books as a "billion-dollar funding gap," only "the number in your account is lower than you want." This eliminates concentration risk — with a 401k, pension insolvency can never happen. The cost is that risk shifts from the company to the individual.

30:37 Pensions were actually great clients for Wall Street
The popular story is that the shift from pensions to 401ks was good for Wall Street, because it turned people who would retire on a pension into retail clients trading their own accounts. Levine pushes back: a pension is itself an excellent client for Wall Street, because its time horizon is long and it can make the spicy investments retail investors won't touch — private equity, private credit. The 401k, over these decades, became cheap index funds, and retail investors actually pay extremely low fees. So now the financial industry is pushing to "revive the pension," stuffing private assets into retirement accounts, because charging one basis point on a public equity index earns you nothing.

32:44 Retail says long-term but their hands want liquidity
Private credit BDCs raise money from retail investors on the logic that "you have a 30-year horizon, you don't need liquidity, you should take the liquidity premium." Then this year software companies delivered bad news, investors rushed to redeem, and the BDCs could only say they would allow just 5% of people to redeem each quarter. Levine calls it "psychological liquidity mismatch": the fund really is making long-term investments and really should not sell long-term assets to meet redemptions; but retail investors psychologically want more liquidity than the fund offers. In theory, selling private assets to retirement savers is right; in practice, it is very hard.

item.title: Hard Tech Is One-Fifth of the YC Batch: Software Companies Are Being Eaten by Agents
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ycsp-硬科技占-yc-批次两成-软件公司正在被智能体吃掉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ycsp-硬科技占-yc-批次两成-软件公司正在被智能体吃掉/
item.description: In YC's latest batch, hard tech companies went from 8% to 20%, with robotics, defense, semiconductors and power all doubling or more; meanwhile software companies are shifting from selling tools to selling "getting the job done," and median revenue rose from 8K to 20K.
item.content:encoded:
In YC's latest batch, hard tech companies went from 8% to 20%, with robotics, defense, semiconductors and power all doubling or more; meanwhile software companies are shifting from selling tools to selling "getting the job done," and median revenue rose from 8K to 20K.

This episode is an insider using batch data to explain trends, with concrete numbers and cases on both the hard tech and agent lines. High information density, good for quickly calibrating your judgment.

1:04 Hard tech went from 8% to 20%
Diana analyzed companies YC admitted over the last 18 to 12 months: hard tech's share rose from 8% to 20%. Broken out: robotics from 1% to 6-7%, industrial manufacturing from 4% to 10%, defense from 1.5% to 5%, semiconductors and photonics from 1% to nearly 4%, power infrastructure from 1% to nearly 3%. Across the physical atom stack these numbers generally tripled to quintupled. Over the same period, the median YC company had zero revenue when admitted; in past batches median monthly revenue was about 8K by demo day, now it's 20K.

3:04 The share of technical founders is rising
Jared mentioned that in the current summer batch, one in every six founders has a PhD, far above historical levels. The reason is that working on things like silicon photonics usually requires a strong research background. Gary added that hard tech used to be hard because supply chains and software engineering were the limiting factors; now with codegen, top-tier full-stack hardware no longer requires hiring a thousand excellent engineers — one or two people, or a small team, is enough, and that changes the economics. The real bull case isn't that investors are avoiding software, it's that the models themselves are accelerating scientific research, letting startups make research breakthroughs earlier.

5:05 Defense and space became the new narrative
Gary said three macro trends are driving atom growth. First, after SpaceX's successful IPO, a generation of founders wants to build space companies — for example Exosat doing sovereign Starlink solutions, and Beyond Reach Labs doing satellite solar panels. Second, this generation of founders grew up in an environment where war was heavily discussed, and they want to do defense. Icarus is building a solar-powered U-2 reconnaissance aircraft that can do surveillance and communications, and has already landed a seven-figure contract with the new Department of War; Nine Mothers does counter-drone defense, a shotgun turret with CV, and special forces are buying it. Third, compute itself is a heavy physical process: the cost of an A100 per hour is rising because demand is too great and supply is insufficient.

8:08 Hardware companies are growing at software speed
Nox Metals is bringing metal manufacturing back to the US, rebuilding the metal supply chain in empty Detroit factories. Its customers are emerging defense tech companies that need metal to build things, and existing suppliers are mostly slow-moving old businesses that can't keep up with the pace of new defense companies. Gary analogized to the early Web 2.0 era: new startups prefer to buy from new startups because they can collaborate at the same speed, like using Stripe instead of traditional credit card providers. PG tweeted that Nox Metals is growing at software speed.

10:12 The compute stack digs from chips down to power
Diana said GPU prices are anomalous: the A100 is already old, yet its cost per hour is still rising because demand exceeds supply. Around data center bring-up — site selection and construction, software, the actual buildout, power supply solutions — there are startups working on all of it. Going down to core compute silicon: Lamb Labs is building a new processor, Bot is building a new custom hardware architecture using ternary representation, because as Nvidia went from A100 to H100 to B300, floating-point precision dropped generation by generation, and LLM architectures don't need full-precision floating point — even FP2 can work. Dipole Labs is building all-optical switches, because electronic switches can't keep up with GPUs and have become the bottleneck in many data centers.

17:16 Systems of record either get eaten or become the harness
Gary's argument: if you're a system of record company, you either get raided — once MCP is released the data moat disappears and switching becomes easy — or you become the harness yourself, the place where people don't just read and write but actually get work done. He cited the RKGI benchmark: the same model plugged into different harnesses performs differently, and model plus harness is what equals output. Some claim Astra with a custom harness exceeds 90% on RKGI 3, when a few months ago that number was in the low double digits.

18:19 The share of software doing complete tasks doubled
Diana said the share of YC-admitted companies doing full-stack end-to-end tasks rose from 10% to more than 25%. The difference is that agents actually do the work, rather than being point solutions that still need a human to operate them, like SaaS five to eight years ago. The fastest-growing ones are exactly these companies doing complete workflows — for example insurance brokerage, clinical intake, medical billing. Jared added that it's been nearly a year since agentic coding became truly usable (Opus 4.5), and these workflows are now blooming across the board; people are willing to pay more for software that "gets the job done."

21:19 Zero to seven-figure revenue in three months
Diana said that this year, for the first time, she saw companies go from zero to seven-figure revenue during the batch, over a span of just three months; in the past this took 18 months or more. Part of the reason is that they're solving real problems, and agentic coding raises product maturity — founders can run 20 coding agent sessions at once. Another fast-growing category is selling data or RL environments to labs, and many of these companies keep a low profile. Over the past two years YC has invested in more than a dozen companies with annual revenue over $10 million selling data or RL environments, many reaching hundreds of millions, with the companies only a few years old.

item.title: The Sweetest Thing May Not Be Sugar but a Beam of Light Shone Into the Brain
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-radiolab-最甜的东西可能不是糖-而是照进脑子的一束光/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-radiolab-最甜的东西可能不是糖-而是照进脑子的一束光/
item.description: Ranked by sweetness, sugar is not the sweetest; but by the sweetness you actually taste, sugar is nearly impossible to beat. More disruptive still: shine a laser directly on sweet neurons and you could, in principle, create a sweetness humans have never tasted.
item.content:encoded:
Ranked by sweetness, sugar is not the sweetest; but by the sweetness you actually taste, sugar is nearly impossible to beat. More disruptive still: shine a laser directly on sweet neurons and you could, in principle, create a sweetness humans have never tasted.

Medium information density, but the back half has real substance: there is only one kind of sweet receptor versus twenty to thirty bitter receptors, and optogenetics can manufacture sweetness directly. Good for a commute.

4:05 The number one spot on the sweetness leaderboard is not sugar
The food industry really does rank sweet molecules, with sucrose as the benchmark. Honey is about 1.5 times sucrose, aspartame about 200 times, the katemfe fruit of the West African rainforest about 2000 times, advantame about 20000 times, and the top-ranked lugduname about 300000 times — a pinch of it can sweeten an entire swimming pool. But Eric Walters says this ranking measures only potency, meaning ‘how little of a thing it takes to light up the sweet receptor’, which is useful to soda and chewing gum makers and is a different question from ‘how sweet it actually tastes’.

8:25 Something 20000 times sweeter, a child spits out
Latif gave his own child the number-two-ranked advantame, and the child spat it on the floor and scraped his tongue with his fingers. Scientists say it is 20000 times sweeter than sugar, yet it does not taste sweet. The reason is that there is only one kind of sweet receptor but twenty to thirty kinds of bitter receptors, so making a molecule that triggers only sweetness and touches no bitter receptor is like tiptoeing through a minefield. That is why so many sugar substitutes carry off-flavors.

10:30 The sweet receptor is a dimmer, not a switch
Paul Breslin of Rutgers says that if you keep adding advantame to water, the sweetness does not keep climbing to the moon but plateaus. The sweet receptor is less like a switch and more like a dimmer: it can get brighter and brighter, but a sugar substitute can only brighten it so far. By the standard of ‘how far you can turn the dimmer up’, Eric Walters says sugar may be the sweetest thing — he has never tasted anything sweeter than sugar. The episode goes all the way around and comes back to the starting point, but for a deep reason: glucose is the brain's best fuel, and the sweet receptor evolved for sugar in the first place.

14:39 Strawberries taste sweeter than blueberries, but blueberries have more sugar
Blueberries actually contain twice the sugar of strawberries, yet strawberries taste sweeter. The mechanism is volatiles: the sugar-free aroma molecules strawberries release are pumped from the back of the mouth into the nasal cavity as you chew and swallow, and these olfactory signals overlap with taste signals in the brain, giving sweetness a boost. Vision works the same way: dye the same sugar red, or shape it to look like fruit, and perceived sweetness rises. Latif did a live experiment with honey plus strawberry flavoring and red coloring, and after tasting it Lulu said it was ‘noticeably sweeter’.

18:43 High notes can push sweetness up another ten percent
In research at the Science Museum in London, certain high-frequency tones raised perceived sweetness by 5% to 10%. Latif played them for Lulu, who said it was ‘more layered, more sparkling, more crystalline’, but she also admitted this step was far subtler than the strawberry one, and that honey left standing crystallizes on its own, which could be a confound. As for why sound affects sweetness, the episode states plainly that no one knows the exact reason; it just keeps showing up in experiments.

21:50 Install a bitter receptor on the sweet pathway
Charles Zuker of Columbia University traced the entire sweet signal path from tongue to brain: tongue to ganglion, to the brainstem, to another station in the brainstem, then to the thalamus, and finally to the cortex — only at the cortex do you say ‘this is sweet’. His experimental method is direct: normally the cells carry sweet receptors, so sweetness activates this pathway; if you swap in bitter receptors there, bitter chemicals will activate the same sweet pathway. He does this not to find the sweetest thing but to understand how sweetness and taste work in the brain, which might help with addiction, obesity, eating disorders and diabetes.

22:50 Use a laser to make a mouse taste a sweetness that isn't there
Zuker's team implanted a light switch only in the sweet-sensing neurons of mice, then inserted an optical fiber into their heads; turn on the laser and those neurons fire, and the brain says ‘sweet’ — even though the animal is eating nothing. Latif pressed him: could you turn the laser all the way up and create a sweetness humans have never tasted? Zuker said that in principle it is imaginable, that you might create the sweetest sweet, and that the sweetest thing could be light. Lulu's reaction was resistance: this amounts to stripping pleasure out of the real world entirely, to the point where you would not even need to leave the house.

25:52 The sugar in raspberries drifts in interstellar dust
A research team at the Center for Astrobiology in Spain observed a cloud of interstellar dust and gas near the center of the Milky Way, read its composition with spectroscopy, and found large amounts of erythrulose — a four-carbon sugar. It was the first time humans had found sugar in deep space, and a relatively complex sugar at that. As it happens, erythrulose also exists in raspberries. From this Latif joked that somewhere there might really be a space raspberry. This segment pushes ‘the sweetest thing’ from the tongue out to the cosmic scale.

item.title: New Housing Fund Rules: Take What You Can, But Don't Treat It as Savings
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-zhixing-公积金新规-能取则取-但别把它当存款/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-zhixing-公积金新规-能取则取-但别把它当存款/
item.description: The housing fund is not savings you can withdraw at will — fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued for repayment and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap, so money you should take, you should still take.
item.content:encoded:
The housing fund is not savings you can withdraw at will — fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued for repayment and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap, so money you should take, you should still take.

Three people in different situations — a self-employed worker, a young professional, a property owner — each run their own numbers, turning the 20 clause changes in the new rules into concrete decisions. The second half, on flexible-employment contributions and the contrast with the public sector, is especially informative.

13:10 Six months after auto-withdrawal, I paused it myself
After Zhou Yi set up Beijing's no-threshold monthly rental withdrawal of 2000 yuan, she found the money slid into another card the moment it arrived, completely decoupled from the mental account for paying rent; when her spending card ran dry at month's end, the money was auto-deducted, which only added friction to daily life. Once she confirmed the housing fund balance earns 1.5% interest, higher than the roughly 0.95% on a one-year bank time deposit, she paused the withdrawal the next day. Yubai points out this contrasts with the advice three years ago to ‘take everything you can, use everything you can’ — two young colleagues in the department have made the same choice. Lao Qian cautions that this is indeed a low-efficiency use of funds, but most people can't achieve the efficiency they imagine for themselves; people just keep fake books for themselves.

21:12 The housing fund is not savings — not being able to take it out is the norm
Yubai walks through an extreme case: a young person loses their job and goes home with no liquid funds, tens of thousands of yuan sitting in the housing fund, but the home is owner-occupied, so it qualifies neither as buying nor as renting; even if the new rules allow withdrawal under the heading of renovation or property fees, if the family has no such needs, there's nothing to be done. If you take the risk and invent a pretext for fraudulent withdrawal, you'll be pursued to return the entire amount and barred from withdrawing any housing fund for three years. So both approaches hold — ‘take everything you can’ and ‘treat it as forced savings at a rate above demand deposits’ — and the key is the individual's situation.

23:43 The new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order
This revision adjusts 20 clauses in total. First, renovating an owner-occupied home and paying property fees on an owner-occupied home are included as withdrawal purposes for the first time; the housing fund no longer serves only loan-based home purchases. Second, rental withdrawal used to require that rent exceed a set proportion of household wage income; this version removes that restriction, and renting is placed first in the withdrawal order. Third, flexible-employment workers are formally brought into the system for the first time: self-employed individuals and part-time workers may contribute voluntarily and apply for housing fund loans. In addition, the management center should reply to withdrawal applications within three days and to loan applications within ten days, and nationwide mutual recognition of contribution records is being pushed forward.

30:18 The share of housing fund money lent out has fallen from 70% to 30%
The figure Lao Qian saw: this year, the share of housing fund contributions lent out is as low as just over 30%, against more than 70% at the peak — a steady decline in just a few years. In other words, the theoretically most stable, lowest-rate, highest-quality lending channel is actually used by only a bit over 30% of people. That directly reflects how low the willingness to buy is. Lao Qian also notes the new rules point toward housing consumption rather than leverage: renting moved to first place, property fees and renovation are withdrawable, thresholds dropped sharply — supporting measures as the real estate market shifts from an incremental to a stock phase, and also echoing the aging trend: the monthly uptick in withdrawal share began in 2023, exactly matching the retirement of the 1960s cohort.

32:20 If you want to buy, be careful about withdrawing your housing fund
Yubai warns: housing fund loan limits are tied to account balance — in some cities you can borrow 16 times the balance, in others 20 times, varying by city. Guangzhou has several caps; at application, the smallest of the applicable standards governs — for a first or second owner-occupied home the minimum down payment is 20%, so on a 1 million yuan home the loan cannot exceed 800,000; and a monthly repayment exceeding 50% of monthly income also fails. So before withdrawing your housing fund as living expenses, check your city's loan rules. Yubai is also cautious about the buy-side logic that ‘the rental yield is close to the housing fund rate, you're only short a down payment’: you still have to weigh depreciation, price swings, and how to withstand risk once a 600,000 down payment is locked up.

44:05 Flexible-employment contributors carry the full amount alone
For flexible-employment workers the contribution base and rate are calculated the same way as for employees, but no employer pays half, so one person bears the full 10% to 24%. The base must be self-declared: below 10,000 no proof is needed; above 10,000 you must log into the individual income tax app and pull your tax details as documentation, to prevent inflating the base to extract a higher loan limit. Zhou Yi ran the numbers: 10,000 at 10% to 24% is 1,000 to 2,400 yuan, and this money is not counted toward individual income tax, but it's a loss if you never use it. In addition, most pilot cities require 6 to 12 consecutive months of contributions before you can apply for a housing fund loan, and most do not allow one-time back-payment.

47:33 In the public sector, the housing fund is invisible welfare
Zhou Yi asked a friend back home with a public-institution post, who readily showed a screenshot of her housing fund account: the monthly deposit is more than twice Zhou Yi's, and the balance already exceeds her savings; the friend lives at home with no rental need, so the housing fund just accumulates as forced savings or future loan capacity, plus she has an occupational annuity, and the contribution base counts bonuses and subsidies in full. Lao Qian adds: the housing fund is tax-free, and on top of that individual pension contributions are capped at 12,000 yuan a year and taxed at 3% on withdrawal — so the public sector already has an extra layer of tax advantage. On the data: in 2025 the national average annual wage for urban non-private unit employees was 129,441 yuan, versus 71,590 yuan for private units — while working hours run the other way.

52:44 Full housing fund contributions are a slice for judging a company
Lao Qian's judgment on whether ‘a company that pays the housing fund is a more desirable choice’ has not changed at all: a company that pays the housing fund in full respects its employees and respects the rules, which means it is probably well-run across the board, rather than finding workarounds for every policy. He goes further: this points to not making profit maximization the first goal, to treating people as people, and the invisible returns show up elsewhere. Zhou Yi has run the numbers: on a wage base of 100, you actually take home just over 70, but the boss pays out over 130 — everyone along the chain feels aggrieved. Lao Qian cites Ford's Model T wage increase — letting workers afford a car and have time to use it wasn't capitalist conscience, it was simply a better utility function.

item.title: AI Executives Line Up to Ask for Regulation: Even the Accelerationists Are Getting Spooked
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-hardfork-ai-高管集体求监管-连加速派也开始发怵/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-hardfork-ai-高管集体求监管-连加速派也开始发怵/
item.description: Dario Amodei calls for resident evaluators inside AI companies, with Altman, Musk and Hassabis following — competitors who agree on almost nothing are, for the first time, saying publicly what they have said privately for years.
item.content:encoded:
Dario Amodei calls for resident evaluators inside AI companies, with Altman, Musk and Hassabis following — competitors who agree on almost nothing are, for the first time, saying publicly what they have said privately for years.

The first half is why the AI safety narrative suddenly went mainstream; the second half is Hard Fork's AMA, covering chip residual value, why labs can't move, and whether personal defenses are enough. Medium information density; the AMA portion is more casual chat.

4:05 The resignation post tore open an internal consensus
Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic and OpenAI, saying publicly that neither company is acting responsibly and that they are "racing straight to self-improving super intelligence." What actually made Casey realize he was inside a bubble was the reply from Anthropic employee Evan Hubinger: he too believes AI could kill all humans, and puts the probability above 10%. Casey's reaction was "that's it?" — among the lab researchers he talks to, a 10% PDOOM counts as optimistic. For the first time, outsiders started asking: if you all believe this yourselves, why are you still doing it.

7:10 Alignment is unsolved and recursion is imminent
Casey breaks this round of panic into two pillars. The first is the alignment problem exposed by the Hugging Face incident: researchers had assumed that dangerous behavior between agents — mutual sacrifice, mutual cooperation — would show up much later, but they saw it in still very primitive models. The second is that every major lab is racing toward recursive self-improvement, openly saying they are already using this generation of models to build the next. An unsolved alignment problem plus imminent recursive self-improvement is what makes the resignations look reasonable rather than a cult shouting apocalypse.

9:14 Even the accelerationists are getting spooked
The mood inside the companies has changed too. Three or four months ago, the same company held both a safety and alignment team worried about risk and a team that just improved model capabilities and chased new breakthroughs, and the two sides were opposed. What has changed in the past few weeks: even the optimists, the accelerationists, the capability people are starting to be frightened by the pace of system progress. That is what makes this round different from past AI risk narratives — not that external critics multiplied, but that the people internally who worried least have started to worry.

10:17 Dario wants to put regulators inside the companies
Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word piece, "We Must Pace the Frontier," calling for globally coordinated AI slowdown and proposing a concrete mechanism: embedded evaluators inside major AI companies, given employee-level access and stationed in the office to continuously monitor whether systems show dangerous capabilities or sabotage behavior. He said Anthropic would do it first, without waiting for industry or regulators to force it. The model is the arrangements that already exist in banking. Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis then said they would follow — Altman and Amodei agree on almost nothing normally.

16:30 An industry asking for regulation is highly abnormal
Casey says he has been unexpectedly optimistic these past few weeks. Not because the technology got safer, but because these competing AI leaders, who normally won't give each other the time of day, are now willing to say publicly what they have said privately for years. That gives their own employees permission to speak up, and gives legislators permission to take it seriously — few industries go to Washington and say "please slow us down, we're out of control, regulate us before it's too late." He stresses this is different from the social media era: Facebook never once said "our recommendation algorithm is addictive, please slow us down."

21:58 Everyone already has the recipe
Kevin adds an easily overlooked fact: everyone has the recipe for large language models, everyone knows how to build one. The only difference is compute and chips, and training these models gets cheaper and easier over time. So even if you fully trust OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and xAI, the problem remains — before long, six or seven kids in some country can put together their own out-of-control agent swarm and let it loose. This is not a one-country problem for the US; the cat is already out of the bag. That is also why you act while there are only five near-frontier labs.

1:00:05 Chips don't become worthless in three or four years
Asked whether companies should slow down and hold budget given that smaller, faster chips are coming in 2027 and 2028, Kevin's analogy is that last year's chip is like last year's iPhone: the resale value is still high and it can still do a lot. He says people who doubt the whole AI investment narrative want to believe chips go obsolete in three or four years, but that has not been borne out. Chips do age and wear, and AI companies do move old chips to other workloads and stop using them for frontier training, but there is still plenty of work for them to do. They even had a company (unnamed) send over a very old chip to put on display in their new office.

1:02:08 AI labs can't move because of network effects
Someone asked why OpenAI and Anthropic don't move their model-release base to the UK or EU, given that US regulation and export controls are an existential threat. Kevin's judgment is blunt: if Trump won't let them release frontier models in the US, he also won't let them export the whole lab to another country, even though someday they would very much like to. Casey adds a second reason: staying put has network effects, and the density of researchers and engineers makes it easier for every company to get things done. Moving elsewhere would save a lot of money and might help on regulation, tax and export controls, but it would lose the feeling of being at the center of this boom — a boom that looks virtual but is still highly concentrated geographically.

item.title: Stablecoins Are Not a Duopoly: Big Companies Want Their Own Coin
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-empire-稳定币不是双寡头-大公司要发自己的币/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-empire-稳定币不是双寡头-大公司要发自己的币/
item.description: The multi-stablecoin debate returns: Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins, Circle's USDC network effect is underrated, but if rates fall to 2-3% its revenue gets cut in half.
item.content:encoded:
The multi-stablecoin debate returns: Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins, Circle's USDC network effect is underrated, but if rates fall to 2-3% its revenue gets cut in half.

Regulation, stablecoins, Circle Arc, the Meta vs Instinct fight, Polymarket's talent war — high information density, and the back half is worth more than the front half.

4:05 The multi-stablecoin debate is not over
Santi previously said the ‘hundreds of stablecoin thesis is dead’, and Rob pushed back on the spot. Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins; SoFi, Verve, two bank consortia, the Stripe consortium, MoneyGram and Western Union are all doing it, and Bridge already has its own stablecoin internally for treasury management. His mechanism: big companies hold a lot of cash, and if they can earn yield on it, they have an incentive to issue their own coin rather than use USDC or USDT. Santi pressed: don't these big companies have FX desks at JP Morgan and Morgan Stanley? Rob said it depends on the size of the company and the complexity of global treasury management — Western Union's remittance corridors in Africa and Latin America are something JP Morgan's correspondent banking network can't do well.

13:18 CLARITY failed, but nobody has really given up
The Senate voted down the CLARITY Act 49 to 50 on Tuesday; it needed 60 votes. Three Republicans — Susan Collins, Josh Hawley and Jerry Moran — voted against, and every Democrat they had been counting on voted against. Santi said not to over-read Tillis's turn, since Kirsten Gillibrand said that same day she is still pushing the legislation. On Polymarket the odds of passage fell as low as 4% at one point, then came back to 8%. The market sold off on the news, with Coinbase down 10% and Circle down 12%. Rob said it's worth remembering that dozens of people worked on this bill for a year, including staff on the Banking Committee and the Agriculture Committee.

16:58 The SEC gives tokenized stocks a five-year exemption
The SEC issued an order granting tokenized securities trading venues (TSVS) a five-year interim conditional exemption, letting them trade tokenized NMS stocks through permissioned AMMs and liquidity pools without registering as exchanges, and liquidity providers got a limited market-maker exemption. Two key conditions: token holders must get the same rights as holders of the underlying stock, such as dividends and voting; and third-party tokenization requires written notice and giving the issuer a chance to object. Santi read that out and said this clause could directly break the current onchain tokenized stock practice — if AMC can object, you can't just throw AMC onto Hyperliquid. Rob said this is almost certainly coming, because onchain tokenized stocks currently create strange dislocations after hours and pre-market, and Robinhood pairing memecoins with tokenized stocks is an example.

22:43 The winner in tokenization is the whole ecosystem
Rob said it's hard to point to a single winner. The obvious beneficiaries are issuers, existing exchanges and clearinghouses, new exchanges that want into the US market (Coinbase, Polymarket, Lighter, Hyperliquid, Backpack), global neobanks, and new transfer agents and core infrastructure providers such as Alpaca. Santi said his first reaction was Superstate and Securitize, and Securitize was up 16% that day. Rob said this looks more like a rising tide lifting all boats than value concentrating in one place. He added that as more assets come onchain, everything onchain gets bigger — more liquidity, more users, better infrastructure, more stablecoin issuance.

29:06 S&P buying Open Zeppelin is buying data
S&P is a ratings agency with a roughly $120 billion market cap and about $14 billion in revenue; this week it first led Kao's Series B extension (Kao raised its Series B four years ago, and this time may have raised about $50 million, bringing the B round to about $110 million, with investors including RBC, DRW, Broadridge, BNP and Nasdaq), then acquired smart contract security firm Open Zeppelin. Rob said the acquisition surprised him, since Open Zeppelin doesn't seem like a company that would run a process to sell itself. His read: S&P gives ratings, and it can use Open Zeppelin for real-time risk benchmarks and data, to assess what happens inside protocols, and then sell that to clients. Santi said he heard this is the first such deal, and that traditional capital markets data and analytics players (Moody's and others) will do more of the same. Rob said many crypto companies raised a lot of money and have good products but aren't good enough as standalone businesses, and companies like S&P grow into conglomerates by constantly buying good niche products and then bundling them for you through a terminal.

37:40 Circle pushing memes on Arc's first day was a misstep
Circle launched Arc, with more than 190 partners on day one and over $220 million of TVL pre-seeded in a Morpho vault. Rob said he doesn't understand why Circle came out pushing a bunch of memes on day one, since Arc had always been positioned as a payments-first chain, talking about agentic finance, privacy, FX liquidity and real business activity. He said this is the exact opposite of the story Circle has told for a long time, and it left a lot of people with a bad impression. Santi said he went to Circle's launch event yesterday, and the room and Twitter were two completely different worlds — within an hour he met people from BlackRock, DTCC, ICE, Visa and MoneyGram, and Circle's convening power is extremely strong; if it had launched purely on its original positioning, the effect would have been much better. Rob said Circle may have been looking at the success of Robinhood chain, but Robinhood is a trading platform and Circle is a payments company, and having bought Taza Pay it should stay in its own lane.

42:38 Circle's revenue gets cut in half by rates
Rob said he doesn't expect 4% to 4.5% rates to last forever, and that rates will normalize to between 2% and 3%, which means that if Circle is just an interest-income business, its revenue at the current TVL gets cut in half. He also said that as a payments stablecoin, if it can't share yield with end customers, there isn't much reason to hold large amounts of it. Circle's agreement with Coinbase requires giving 50% to Coinbase, which puts it at a disadvantage competing with new stablecoins. So Circle is working hard to become a payments company and get a payments company multiple, and Arc and the Circle Payment Network are both part of that story. Santi said not to underestimate USDC's network effect — in DeFi there is now only one thing that matters for liquidity, and that's USDC; any DeFi founder needs USDC on their platform.

46:14 Instinct's reckoning comes in month four
Rob said companies are now getting bigger faster and raising more money faster, that venture capital as a market structure is broken, and that the hottest companies see valuations rise faster and faster regardless of fundamentals. He said a company's first big reckoning usually comes in year four, but Instinct's first big reckoning will come in month four — because the two biggest companies in the world are about to launch direct competitors, Grokbot and Meta's Muse. Santi said in his own use Muse is six to eight times better than Instinct; Instinct is clearly compute-constrained, and for the same question Muse is sometimes 10 to 15 minutes faster, fails less often, and can route around the roadblocks Resy has set up for these products. Rob said he doesn't know how growth investors are comfortable at this valuation, and the only thing that could prove them wrong is Instinct sprinting to train its own model, but that takes a billion dollars to build data centers.

item.title: Prediction Markets Aren't a Casino, but 90% of Volume Comes From Sports
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freakonomics-预测市场不是赌场-但九成交易量来自体育/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freakonomics-预测市场不是赌场-但九成交易量来自体育/
item.description: Kalshi traded four years of compliance for 90% market share, but its revenue structure looks more like a sportsbook; what's genuinely underrated are the quiet markets like FDA approvals.
item.content:encoded:
Kalshi traded four years of compliance for 90% market share, but its revenue structure looks more like a sportsbook; what's genuinely underrated are the quiet markets like FDA approvals.

The first half is founder narrative; the value is in the middle and back: how contracts are written, sports at 90%, regulatory risk. Worth listening for anyone who wants to understand the mechanics of prediction markets.

8:16 Comply for four years first, then open your first market
Kalshi's two founders wrote "regulatory first" into the company's principles and spent four years getting regulatory approval before launching their first market. Mansoor says this is anti-Silicon Valley: others build the product first and patch in compliance later, whereas they asked the federal government up front how the thing should be regulated. The cost was that for the first four years they thought about quitting almost every day, held together by "the cost of regret is too high." The payoff: in 2024 a federal appeals court ruled Kalshi could list election contracts, landing just before the presidential election. Mansoor attributes their 90% market share directly to this path: institutions would rather plug into a platform inside the system, because changing the rules from outside the system is harder.

15:36 Prediction markets force you to shut up, not to take a position
Robin Hanson lays out three mechanisms that make prediction markets more accurate than polls or expert interviews. First, people being interviewed have an incentive to be interesting, dramatic, and to tell the questioner what they want to hear, while the market only rewards being right. Second, the market gives you an incentive to shut up about topics you don't understand — you only bet on the few markets where you genuinely have an edge, whereas interviewees will answer confidently about things they don't know. Third, the market doesn't require you to have a direct opinion on a topic; it invites you to find mispricings and errors in other people's pricing, and pays you to correct them. He closes with an old poker-table line: sit down and look for the sucker; if you can't find him, you're the sucker — so don't play that market.

20:48 Internal prediction markets die on the project owner's excuse
Eli Lilly ran an internal prediction market in the early 2000s that successfully predicted which drug compounds would pass Phase III trials; Google ran one called Google Profit. Both were considered effective, and neither survived. Hanson's explanation: the project owner wants to know whether they'll deliver on time, but what they want even more is a good excuse if they fail. And the best excuse is precisely "everything was going fine and then at the last minute something nobody could have foreseen happened." A market that continuously and accurately predicts whether you'll be late invalidates that excuse in advance, so nobody wants it to exist.

22:58 Domain expertise is not the key skill for forecasting the future
Mansoor cites Philip Tetlock's Superforecasting research: put experts in a given domain (say, geopolitics) up against a group of non-experts forecasting the same set of events, and the non-experts win. His explanation is that domain experts become too doctrinaire over time, while people who can step back and look at a problem coolly are better calibrated and less biased. Mansoor says this is a fairly heretical claim in politics, academia, and financial analysis circles — it implies that if you want a more accurate answer, you should look for a diverse group of participants who pride themselves on self-calibration, critical reading, and filtering information, not an authority in some field. He treats this as Kalshi's underlying logic.

33:28 One contract takes a month to write, for grammar and apostrophes
Nicole Kagan writes the contracts and self-certifies them with the CFTC. The most complex category is "what someone will say in a given speech," and they recently rewrote the rules because a pile of grammar questions came up: what if there's an apostrophe? If they misspeak or mispronounce it, does it still count as the same word? What if it appears inside a proper noun? What if the livestream cuts out midway and it's uploaded somewhere else afterward? Those rules took over a month to write, seven or eight pages, extremely detailed. When Bloomberg reported on it, they guessed the rules were for automated processing and must be for AI; Kagan says that's not it at all — they wrote them so users could understand, and never considered that "something a human can understand is probably something a computer can understand too."

35:35 When you can't call a winner, settle at the last fair price
Kalshi contracts are usually binary: pay $1 if the event happens, $0 if it doesn't, with every position fully collateralized — if one side bets 30 cents, someone must bet 70 cents. But some cases can't be judged yes or no. Cardi B was visibly dancing during her seven-second Super Bowl halftime cameo, but she had no mic and it couldn't be confirmed whether she was singing, so the team said "we are epistemologically uncertain" and settled at the last fair price. Another case is 50-50: when multiple people win simultaneously, each settles at 50 cents. Kagan says they have the right to do this when it's genuinely unclear whether an event meets the criteria, and they've already revised the halftime contract — the new rules require an audible lead or backing vocal, and under the new rules Cardi B didn't perform.

41:52 90% of volume comes from sports, and that's the most uncomfortable fact
Dubner puts it directly: roughly 90% of Kalshi's volume is concentrated in a category barely mentioned until then — sports, the business that makes DraftKings and FanDuel nervous. Mansoor's response is that sports' share is falling fast and other categories are growing faster, but he concedes "10% is also a lot, don't forget we're big." He insists on distinguishing gambling from trading: all derivatives markets are mostly speculative, speculation provides liquidity, and the key isn't whether there's speculation but the business model — one model hunts for losers and bans winners, the other pursues price discovery and wants smart people to come in. He also concedes the second model carries risk, saying there's "responsible gambling" and "responsible trading," and platforms have a responsibility to monitor.

44:00 70-80% of active users never place an order
Mansoor says one of his favorite numbers is that 70% to 80% of active users don't trade — they just log in every day, keep it next to X and a few newspapers, and use it to calibrate or check information. Kalshi's business model is a neutral platform, like the NYSE or Nasdaq, taking an average 1% on trades and not caring who wins or loses. He also says the information environment is getting more polarized and the signal-to-noise ratio is falling, because social media algorithms reward clickbait: a nuanced, restrained, multi-paragraph take gets four likes on X, while something extreme and unhinged gets tens of thousands; prediction markets have exactly the opposite incentive — the nuanced, boring, well-calibrated judgment is the one that makes money.
