item.title: Diffusion isn't just for images — it's going to win at inference for language models
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-nopriors-扩散模型不是图像专利-它要在推理时赢下语言模型/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-nopriors-扩散模型不是图像专利-它要在推理时赢下语言模型/
item.description: Autoregressive inference must generate one token at a time sequentially, which is a memory bandwidth bottleneck; diffusion models process multiple tokens in parallel at once, and the inference workload looks more like training, so Inception is betting on it.
item.content:encoded:
Autoregressive inference must generate one token at a time sequentially, which is a memory bandwidth bottleneck; diffusion models process multiple tokens in parallel at once, and the inference workload looks more like training, so Inception is betting on it.

A diffusion model pioneer explains clearly why parallelism at the inference stage will become the architectural deciding factor, and how a 50-person company finds differentiation in the cracks between giants.

3:10 Diffusion models started because GANs were too unstable
Ermon says that when he was working on image generation back then, he was very dissatisfied with GANs: they worked, but training was extremely unstable and results were hard to reproduce. So in 2019 he and his PhD students turned to score-based generative models, with the idea of training a neural network to denoise — if it can denoise, it means it understands image structure, and it can then reverse the process to progressively refine a clean image from pure noise. This is the underlying technology of modern diffusion models. He emphasizes that today's best image, video, some music, and a large number of protein models are all based on diffusion.

5:11 The 2024 paper brought diffusion to text
Ermon's team published a paper in 2024 that, for the first time at GPT-2 scale (under a billion parameters), got diffusion models to match the quality of autoregressive models: same perplexity, same degree of data fit, but about 10x faster generation, because diffusion outputs multiple tokens at once. He says this is still somewhat academic, but it was enough for him to decide to start a company and scale the technology to commercial scale.

8:14 Autoregressive inference is a memory bandwidth bottleneck
Ermon analogizes the 2017 switch from RNNs to transformers to the inference stage: during training, transformers won by processing multiple tokens in parallel, but at inference time autoregressive models are still sequential — before generating the 10th token, all previous tokens must be generated first. This workload is extremely memory-bandwidth-bound, with most time spent moving weights between memory hierarchies, very little arithmetic, and it's unfriendly to GPUs. Diffusion models' inference workload looks more like training — processing multiple tokens in parallel at once — so it naturally matches the computation patterns GPUs are good at.

10:16 Inference efficiency also determines the ceiling for RL post-training
Ermon points out that economics is determined by how much intelligence you can get per watt and per dollar. Much of the progress in reasoning models comes from test-time compute scaling, and one of the bottlenecks in RL post-training is generating rollouts — letting the model explore, scoring trajectories, and then improving the model. So inference efficiency directly bottlenecks post-training efficiency: a model that scales better at inference will automatically scale better during post-training. This is the core logic of his bet on diffusion LLMs, and what he calls "more parallel approaches will eventually win."

12:19 Mercury benchmarks against Haiku, Flash, mini series
Ermon says Inception's Mercury model benchmarks against speed-optimized models like Haiku, Flash, mini nano, with comparable quality but significantly faster, and is already serving customers in production. He emphasizes that you can't just run a diffusion LLM on vLLM or SGLang; you must build your own serving engine to handle the complexity of real production workloads. This is both a barrier and a moat: even if someone else trains a diffusion LLM, without a corresponding serving engine they can't use it.

17:21 Voice customer switched from custom chips back to Nvidia GPUs
Ermon gives the example of voice agent company OpenCall: the voice pipeline includes ASR, an inference LLM for tool calls, and TTS, and speed is critical. OpenCall originally served the LLM on Cerebras custom chips to achieve the required speed, then switched to Inception's diffusion LLM because they could get the same speed on Nvidia GPUs — higher availability, lower cost, better quality. Ermon says once you get used to fast models you can't go back, like broadband.

25:26 Diffusion models are inherently more controllable than autoregressive
Ermon says diffusion models are generally easier to control than autoregressive models: autoregressive must wait until the entire object is generated before knowing whether it satisfies constraints, whether it's aligned, what score the reward function gives; diffusion is coarse-to-fine generation, so from early on you can judge whether the direction is right, and you can use external reward functions or constraint sets to guide generation. There's a lot of evidence in the academic literature supporting this, and some guidance methods simply can't be done on autoregressive models. He sees this as the differentiation space for future product experiences.

29:29 20% to 30% of tasks are extremely latency-sensitive
Ermon estimates based on OpenRouter's task classification (research, chat, coding, software engineering, log processing, etc.) that about 20% to 30% of tasks are very latency-sensitive. As a lower bound, this portion of the workload can be served by the model that provides the highest quality within a given latency budget. He also admits that we haven't yet reached frontier intelligence levels, and many workloads still require frontier-level intelligence, so the addressable market for diffusion models is layered.

item.title: When Your Kids Fight, Be a Witness, Not a Judge
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-raisinggh-孩子打架时-当证人别当法官/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-raisinggh-孩子打架时-当证人别当法官/
item.description: Fair isn't equal: give each child what they need, not the identical thing. A parent's job isn't to rule on who's right, but to describe what happened and let them find the next step.
item.content:encoded:
Fair isn't equal: give each child what they need, not the identical thing. A parent's job isn't to rule on who's right, but to describe what happened and let them find the next step.

Medium information density, but three frameworks — "witness, not judge," "fair isn't equal," and "forced apology isn't repair" — are concrete and actionable, well suited to parents with more than one child.

3:05 Deal with your own sibling baggage first
The episode opens by saying: before you intervene, sort out your own emotions. Everyone carries sibling baggage — even people without siblings carry a longing for that relationship, or relief at not having it. The fairness trap is what most easily sets parents off: a piece of cake, a looser rule, a new dress from childhood all leave behind a memory of "I got cheated." Those feelings get summoned the moment you step into your kids' conflict. So the core instruction is: you are a witness, not a judge. The moment you start ruling, the judgment comes from your own history, not from the two children in front of you.

5:07 When you must step in: danger, power imbalance, deadlock
There are three criteria: if a child is in danger, step in; if there's a power imbalance, step in; if they're stuck in a dead loop, step in. If the two are evenly matched and both safe, you can step back and occasionally ask, "Is everyone okay?" What deserves special vigilance is a power dynamic that turns into toxic bullying — rare, but when it happens, an adult has to cut it off. The episode stresses that kids who are bullied by peers or siblings have significantly worse outcomes as adults, and the damage is far more serious than we realize. But bullying has a strict definition: a power difference, repetition, malice, intentional abuse. Merely being "annoying" doesn't count.

6:07 Intervene in sportscaster mode, don't ask who started it
If you have to step in, use "sportscaster mode": like a commentator, describe only the facts you saw — "I noticed this happened over here, did I get that right?" That validates both children at once, takes no side, and produces no winner. Questions to avoid include "Who started it," "Why are you always like this," and "There's just something wrong with you." The episode draws a key distinction: telling a child "what you did was inconsiderate" and telling a child "you're stupid" are two different things. The latter attacks a person's worth and gets a child to bind their anger and emotional outbursts to "I'm not worth anything as a person." The moment you hear dehumanizing language — even mid-screaming, mid-scuffle — pause it on the spot and demand a different way of saying it.

9:13 Under two, protect the little one without making the big one hate him
Under two, you only need to protect the younger one, while trying not to alienate the older one. The older child is already processing "the baby stole my attention," and then gets told "this is your best friend, don't you love him?" — what he's thinking is "No, I don't love him," though sometimes he does. So tell him plainly: you can be angry at your sibling and love him deeply at the same time, you can dislike him today and still love him very much — that's called mixed feelings, and it's completely normal. Also explain: protecting the little one's body is the adult's job, because he can't get out of the way himself, so sometimes I'll pick him up and carry him off. That kind of intervention doesn't heighten the tension, and it isn't saying who's better or worse — only who needs protection from real danger.

14:28 Fair isn't equal — it's giving each child what they need
The single most useful thing in prevention mode: fair isn't equal — not equality, but equity. You give each child what he needs, not the identical thing. The episode gives a concrete example: giving two kids peanut-butter cupcakes the same size, same recipe, same flavor looks perfectly equal, but one of them is allergic to peanuts — so it isn't fair. You can give him vanilla, making sure both kids get a cupcake, but not the same cupcake. This framework applies directly to challenges like "Why does my sister get a phone at twelve and I don't": you are different people, I've learned more since then, so I made a different decision.

16:31 Don't label your kids — labels follow them for life
A shared label for all the kids can promote good behavior — telling your children "you're helpers" produces more helping behavior. But labeling only one child in the house as "the helper" creates tension and a problematic dynamic. The episode says labeling builds a dynamic that, to put it dramatically, "clings to them." Teachers, friends, other people's parents, relatives all label them, so a parent's job is to counteract that damage, because labels bring resentment, insecurity, lack of motivation, and tension between siblings that needn't be as distant as it becomes.

18:41 Forced apology isn't repair — it's fake repair
Repair doesn't require a formal apology. Kids who are fighting suddenly giggle together, share an inside joke, make faces at each other — that is repair, that is reconnecting, and you're watching it happen. Every reconnection reinforces the relationship and tells them this foundation is permanent: it gets messy, but we always come back. But if you feel you have to force an apology, the episode is explicit: an apology isn't repair unless it genuinely comes from the heart, from really feeling you did wrong and wanting to make it up to the other person. Saying "I'm sorry," and saying "Apologize to your brother," are neither of them what the scientific literature calls repair. Fake repair can't build a strong foundation. What you can ask is: "How do you think that made your sibling feel? What could you do to make him feel better?" If the child says nothing, you don't drop it — you come back and ask again a little later.

23:55 Be curious about the instigator, don't just punish him
When one child really is repeatedly stirring things up, first let the other kids know you see them: "I've noticed your sister started it the last few times, and I also see how hard you're trying not to fight — that's hard, let's keep practicing." With the instigator, get genuinely curious first: why is he stirring things up this often? Does he need more one-on-one time? Is there some longing, jealousy or need you haven't noticed? Try to meet it without depriving the other kids. If you just yell "you always start it" and punish him, you don't teach him the underlying skill, and you don't teach him self-reflection — "Why do I keep starting this? What do I actually want?" Teaching a child to figure out what he wants and get it in a productive way is one of the most important things there is. Going after it by stirring up trouble loses most of the time.

item.content:encoded:
Half the rise in US income inequality comes from pass-through business income, and the owners of these businesses aren't tech giants — they're car dealers, beer distributors, dentists and hot dog vendors, protected as "small business" for forty years.

A new study built on linked IRS full tax-return data pulls "who the rich are" away from the tech narrative and back to regional middle-market businesses. High information density, suited to anyone tracking taxes, PE and wealth distribution.

6:13 Tax returns assemble a different picture of the rich
More than a decade ago, the two authors were commissioned by the Treasury to link corporate tax returns with the returns of owners and employees, because even the IRS couldn't match the different forms belonging to the same business. They found that the picture of the rich painted by the media and by Capital in the Twenty-First Century is very different from the actual picture in US tax returns: not passive rent-collecting Gilded Age monopolists, but millions of actively operating middle-market regional business owners. This data project later became the basis of the whole book.

12:16 Seventy percent of pass-through income flows to the top 1%
Of pass-through business income, 70 cents of every dollar flows to the top 1% of earners. From the 1980s to 2021, more than half of the growth in the top 1%'s income share came from pass-through business income. So if you want to understand income inequality and wealth inequality, you can't get around this sector. The authors originally assumed monopolistic giants were passively collecting the money, but found instead middle-market regional businesses spread across the whole country, numbering in the millions.

15:22 Car dealers are the single biggest bucket of pass-through income
The book opens with a "wedding of the century": a third-generation Mercedes dealer in Florida threw his daughter's wedding in Paris, renting out Versailles for the dinner, spending $60 million — right after selling the dealership for several hundred million dollars. When the authors looked at top 0.1% pass-through income by industry, car dealers ranked first. They then checked yacht and private jet registration data and found these people by name, because tax returns themselves can't identify individuals.

19:23 Car dealer wealth is half skill, half license
The authors tell two stories. Larry Miller started in Toyota's parts division, took the parts business from 961st to first, and later owned more than 40 dealerships and bought the Utah Jazz — a good case of "move slow and make things." But the other side is regulatory protection: franchise laws were meant to protect small dealers from being force-fed inventory by Ford and GM, yet in 2008 Chrysler had three times as many dealerships as Toyota while selling the same number of cars, and closing a store meant paying three years' rent. Dealers also enjoy geographic monopolies and high margins on add-on services like warranties and financing.

22:25 Beer distributors are a rent-collecting layer left by Prohibition
When you see a truck on the road with Budweiser on it, the truck actually belongs to a distributor, such as Reyes. These distributors sit between brewers and bars, restaurants and grocery stores; state laws require beer to pass through this layer, originally to stop big brewers from controlling production and distribution at the same time. The result is that these "little guys" became big guys, showing up en masse in the private jet data. The authors mention a beer wholesalers' convention in San Antonio where the mayor said he'd never seen so many private jets at the airport.

34:31 Same anesthesiologist, far higher tax burden for the employee
The book compares two anesthesiologists: one runs a private practice through an S-Corp, the other draws a salary from a hospital system. The former treats most of his income as business profit, paying no payroll tax and no uncapped Medicare surtax, even though he bills Medicare heavily. The IRS only requires payroll tax on the "reasonable compensation" portion of wages; anything above that counts as profit. The 2017 reform cut the top pass-through rate from 37% to below 30%, and although it put guardrails on professional services like doctors, by spinning out surgery, ancillary services or real estate, more income can still be shifted into the lower-rate bucket.

38:35 A quarter of federal elected officials are pass-through owners too
The authors say the reason the tax loophole can't be fixed over the long run is that roughly a quarter of federal elected officials are themselves pass-through business owners. Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno is a car dealer, and the Social Security plan he proposed together with Elizabeth Warren is funded by payroll taxes on working-class wages, with no mention at all of these wealthy business owners. The authors argue the most realistic reform isn't abolishing the loophole but capping it by income: for instance, once business income exceeds $1 million or $400,000, you can no longer claim the deduction that cuts the rate from 37% to 30%.

48:52 The owners' share went from four-tenths to five-tenths
Over the past 25 years, 60% of growth in the corporate sector came from the pass-through form, so the pie is getting bigger; at the same time, the share owners take out of the pie rose from a third to 40% to about 50%. Using data from 2001 to 2021, the authors calculate: value added per worker rose from $34,000 to $52,000, a gain of $18,000, of which owners took $15,000. They attribute this to skill scarcity (the US has 30% fewer doctors than the OECD average, with the AMA restricting supply), policy-created scarcity, and the rising value of professional services such as M&A.
